name: 1 Samuel
sourceNote: Written freshly, thought for thought, from the oldest Hebrew, Greek, and Aramaic witnesses (the Masoretic Text with the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Septuagint, and the Samaritan Pentateuch). © 2026 Jose Santiago. All rights reserved.

verses.text: A man named Elkanah{b} lived in the Ephraim hills. His home town was Ramathaim-zophim,{a} and he belonged to the tribe of Ephraim. His father was Jeroham, who was the son of Elihu, who was the son of Tohu, who was the son of Zuph.
Elkanah was married to two women. Hannah{c} was one and Peninnah{d} was the other. Peninnah had borne children, but Hannah never had.
Every year Elkanah left his town and went up to Shiloh{g} to worship Yahweh{e} of Armies{f} and offer a sacrifice. Two sons of Eli{h} served Yahweh there as priests, Hophni{i} and Phinehas.{j}
Whenever Elkanah made his offering, he passed out portions of the meat. Peninnah and all her sons and daughters each received one,
To Hannah, however, he gave twice as much.{k} He loved her dearly, though Yahweh had closed her womb.
Peninnah, her rival, teased her cruelly and made her angry, because Yahweh had kept Hannah from having children.
This went on year after year. Each time they went up to Yahweh’s house, Peninnah picked on her until Hannah cried and refused to eat.
Her husband Elkanah said to her, “Hannah, what are the tears for? Why do you eat nothing? Why is your heart so heavy? Am I not better to you than ten sons would be?”
Once, after they had finished eating and drinking at Shiloh, Hannah got up.{l} Eli the priest was sitting on his seat beside the door of Yahweh’s temple.
She was in deep pain. She wept and prayed to Yahweh.

And she made a promise: “Yahweh of Armies, look at my sorrow. Remember me and do not forget me. Give me a son, and I will hand him over to Yahweh all the days of his life. No razor will ever touch his head.”{m}
While she went on praying to Yahweh, Eli kept his eyes on her mouth.
Hannah was praying silently. Her lips moved, but no sound came out. Eli thought she had been drinking.
“How long will you stay drunk?” he asked. “Put away your wine.”
“No, sir,” Hannah answered. “I am a woman in great sorrow. I have not had any wine or beer. I have been telling Yahweh everything that is in my heart.
Do not count me a wicked woman.{n} Until now I have been speaking from deep trouble and pain.”
“Go in peace,” Eli replied. “May Israel’s God grant the thing you have asked from him.”
“May I always please you,” she said. Then she went off and ate. Her face was no longer sad.{o}
Early next morning they bowed down before Yahweh and then traveled home to Ramah. Elkanah slept with his wife Hannah, and Yahweh did not forget her.
Before long Hannah was expecting, and she gave birth to a boy. “I asked Yahweh for him,” she said, and so she called him Samuel.{p}
The next year Elkanah and his whole family went up to make the yearly sacrifice to Yahweh and keep his promise.
Hannah stayed home. She said to her husband, “When the boy no longer nurses, I will bring him. Then he will stand before Yahweh and live there for good.”{q}

Her husband Elkanah answered, “Do as you think best. Wait until the child is weaned, and may Yahweh bring about what you said.”{r} So she stayed home and fed her boy herself until the day he was weaned.
Once the boy was weaned, she carried him up to Yahweh’s house at Shiloh. With her went a bull three years old,{s} flour measuring half a bushel,{t} and a wineskin. The boy was very young.
After the bull was slaughtered, Hannah led the boy to Eli.
“Excuse me, sir,” she said. “I swear by your life, I am the same woman who was standing next to you here, praying to Yahweh.
It was this boy I was praying for. Yahweh has granted my request.
Now I give him back to Yahweh.{u} As long as he lives, he belongs to Yahweh.” And he{v} bowed down to Yahweh there.

notes.text: Ramathaim-zophim means “two heights of the Zuphites.” In verse 19 the town is called Ramah, “height.” Its exact place is unknown. The Greek Old Testament reads “Armathaim Zipha.”
Elkanah means “God has created” or “God has bought.” The Greek Old Testament spells the names in this family line differently.
Hannah means “favor” or “grace.”
Peninnah may mean “pearl” or “coral.” This is uncertain.
Yahweh is the personal name of Israel’s God (Hebrew YHWH). Many English Bibles use “the LORD” for it. This translation writes the name.
Hebrew Yahweh tsebaot, often “the LORD of hosts.” The armies may be Israel’s forces, the heavenly host, or both. This is the first time the title appears in the Bible.
Shiloh was where the meeting tent stood at this time (Joshua 18:1). It is about 20 miles (32 kilometers) north of Jerusalem.
Eli may mean “high” or “my God.” This is uncertain.
Hophni is probably an Egyptian name. The meaning is uncertain.
Phinehas is an Egyptian name meaning “the Nubian.”

The Hebrew is hard. It says literally “one portion of two faces.” It may mean “a double portion” or “a choice portion.” Some think it means “only one portion.” The Greek Old Testament reads “a choice portion, because she had no child.”
The Greek Old Testament adds “and stood before the Lord.”
The Greek Old Testament adds “and he will drink no wine or strong drink.” Compare the vow in Numbers 6:1-8 and Judges 13:5.
Hebrew “a daughter of Belial,” a way of saying a worthless or wicked person.
The Greek Old Testament reads “and went to her room, and ate and drank with her husband.”
Samuel probably means “name of God” or “heard by God.” Hannah’s words play on the Hebrew verb sha’al, “to ask.” The same verb is the root of the name Saul.
Or “forever.”
So the standard Hebrew text. The Greek Old Testament reads “May the Lord make firm what comes out of your mouth.”
So the Greek Old Testament and other old copies. The standard Hebrew text reads “three bulls,” but verse 25 speaks of only one.
Hebrew “an ephah of flour,” about 6 gallons (22 liters).
Hebrew sha’ul, “asked” or “lent.” It has the same form as the name Saul. The verse plays on the word “ask” in verses 17, 20 and 27.
That is Elkanah, or maybe Samuel. Some Hebrew copies read “they.” The Greek Old Testament reads “and she said” and goes right into Hannah’s song.

verses.text:
Hannah prayed:{a} “My heart is full of joy in Yahweh.
My strength{b} is lifted high by Yahweh.{c}
I laugh at my enemies,
because I am happy that you saved me.

Stop talking so proudly.
Let no boasting leave your lips.
Yahweh is a God who knows,
and he weighs what people do.{e}

The bows of strong soldiers snap,
but the ones who tripped now wear strength like a belt.

The well fed now work for a crust of bread,
and the hungry have all they need.{f}
The woman with no child has seven,
and the mother of many fades away.

Yahweh kills and Yahweh gives life.
He sends people down to the grave{g} and lifts them up.

Yahweh makes one person poor and another rich.
He pushes one down and lifts another up.

He raises the poor out of the dust.
He picks the needy from the ash heap,
giving them a seat among princes
and a place of honor.
Yahweh owns the pillars of the earth,
and he set the world upon them.{h}

He watches over the steps of those who are loyal to him,
but the wicked go silent in the dark.
Nobody wins by strength alone.
Elkanah went back to his home in Ramah. The boy stayed and served Yahweh under Eli the priest.{k}
Eli’s sons were worthless men.{l} They did not respect Yahweh,

They also ignored the share that priests were allowed to take from the people.{m} When a man offered a sacrifice, the priest’s servant came over while the meat boiled, holding a fork with three prongs.
He jabbed it into the pan, kettle, pot, or bowl. The priest kept whatever came up on the fork. They did this to every Israelite who came to Shiloh.

Even ahead of the burning of the fat, the priest’s servant would walk up to the one who was offering and say, “Hand over some meat for the priest’s roasting. He refuses anything boiled. He wants it raw.”
If the man protested, “First let the fat be burned. Then take all you like,” the servant answered, “Hand it over now. If you will not, I will grab it myself.”
The sin of these young men was very serious in Yahweh’s eyes, because they treated Yahweh’s offering with scorn.
But young Samuel served Yahweh, wearing a linen ephod.{n}
Every year his mother sewed him a little robe and carried it up when she and her husband came for the yearly sacrifice.
Eli would bless Elkanah and Hannah with these words: “May Yahweh give you more children from this woman, in return for the boy she lent to Yahweh.”{o} Then they would head home.
Yahweh did visit Hannah. In the end she had three more sons and two daughters. All that time the boy Samuel was growing up in Yahweh’s presence.
Eli was now very old. He kept hearing about all his sons were doing to Israel, and that they slept with the women who served at the door of the meeting tent.{p}
He said to them, “Why do you do such things? I keep hearing about your evil deeds from all the people.
No, my sons. The talk I hear among Yahweh’s people is bad.
If one man wrongs another, God{q} can step in on his behalf. But when a man sins against Yahweh, who can plead his case?” Even so, they paid their father no heed, for Yahweh was set on their deaths.
The boy Samuel kept growing taller. People liked him, and so did Yahweh.
A man of God approached Eli with this word from Yahweh: “I showed myself clearly to the family of your ancestor when they were slaves to Pharaoh in Egypt.{r}
From every tribe in Israel I picked him to be my priest, to climb my altar, to burn incense, and to carry the ephod before me. And I gave his family the Israelites’ food offerings.

Why, then, do you look down on{s} the sacrifices and offerings that I ordered for my dwelling place? You honor your sons above me. You grow fat on the best part of each offering my people Israel bring.’

“So Yahweh, the God of Israel, says: ‘I once promised that your family and your ancestors’ family would serve me forever.’ But now Yahweh says: ‘No more! I honor those who honor me, and those who look down on me will be shamed.
The days are coming when I will cut off your strength{t} and the strength of your family, so that no one in your house lives to be old.
You will watch with envy while good things happen to Israel,{u} and no one in your family will ever grow old.
Any man I leave at my altar will live only to wear out your eyes and bring grief to your heart. And all the children born in your house will die in the prime of life.{w}
You will have a sign: Hophni and Phinehas, your two sons, will die together on a single day.
For myself I will appoint a priest who stays loyal. He will act according to my heart and my mind. I will establish a lasting family for him, and he will serve in front of my chosen king forever.
Whoever is left of your family will come to bow before him and beg for a silver coin{x} or a piece of bread. ‘Put me in some priestly post,’ he will say, ‘so I can eat a morsel of food.’”

notes.text: Hannah’s song (2:1-10) praises God for turning people’s fortunes upside down. Compare Mary’s song in Luke 1:46-55. The Greek Old Testament and a Dead Sea Scroll differ from the standard Hebrew text in several lines.
Hebrew “horn,” a picture of strength taken from the horns of a wild ox.
So the standard Hebrew text. The Greek Old Testament reads “in my God.”
The Greek Old Testament reads “No one is holy like the Lord, and none is just like our God. There is none holy but you.” It does not have the line about the rock.
Or “and he does not weigh what people do,” following the written Hebrew text. The Greek Old Testament reads “and God prepares his own plans.”
The Hebrew is unclear. It says literally “and the hungry stop.” The Greek Old Testament reads “and the hungry have left the land.”
Hebrew Sheol, the place of the dead.
The Greek Old Testament does not have these two lines. It reads, at the start of verse 9, “He gives the prayer of the one who prays, and blesses the years of the righteous.”
So the standard Hebrew text as read aloud. The written text has the singular, “the one who fights him.” The Greek Old Testament reads “The Lord will weaken his enemy. The Lord is holy.”
Hebrew mashiah, “anointed one,” the word that “Messiah” comes from. The Greek Old Testament has a much longer verse here, with words like Jeremiah 9:23-24.
The Greek Old Testament begins the verse, “She left him there before the Lord and went to Armathaim.”
Hebrew “sons of Belial,” meaning worthless or wicked men.
Or “the priests’ custom with the people.” Compare Leviticus 7:31-34 and Deuteronomy 18:3.
This linen ephod was a plain garment worn by those who served at the holy place (compare 22:18; 2 Samuel 6:14). It was not the rich ephod of the high priest in Exodus 28.

So a Dead Sea Scroll and the Greek Old Testament (“for the loan you made to the Lord”). The standard Hebrew text reads “in place of the request he asked of Yahweh.” The word play on “ask” is here again.
The Greek Old Testament leaves out the clause about the women at the door. Compare Exodus 38:8.
Or “the judges” (Hebrew elohim).
The Greek Old Testament reads “when they were slaves in Egypt to the house of Pharaoh.”
The Hebrew is unclear. It says literally “kick at” (compare Deuteronomy 32:15). The Greek Old Testament reads “look on with a shameless eye.”
The arm is a picture of strength.
The Hebrew is unclear. The Greek Old Testament leaves out this line.
So the standard Hebrew text. The Greek Old Testament reads “will fall by the sword of men.”
Hebrew agorah, a small silver coin or weight, a fraction of a shekel. Its exact value is unknown.

verses.text: The boy Samuel served Yahweh under Eli. In those days messages from Yahweh were rare, and visions did not come often.{a}
One night Eli, whose eyes had grown too weak for him to see, was lying down in his own spot.
God’s lamp was still burning.{b} Samuel was sleeping in Yahweh’s temple, close to the chest of God.
Yahweh spoke Samuel’s name,{c} and Samuel replied, “Yes? I am here!”
He hurried to Eli. “Here I am. You called for me.” “No, I did not,” said Eli. “Go back to bed.” So Samuel went back.
Yahweh called a second time, “Samuel!” Again the boy rose and went to Eli. “Here I am. You called for me.” “I did not call, my son,” Eli said. “Lie down again.”
Samuel did not yet know Yahweh. No message from Yahweh had ever been given to him.
A third time Yahweh called. Samuel rose, went to Eli, and said, “Here I am. You called for me.” Now Eli saw that it was Yahweh calling the boy.
Eli instructed Samuel, “Go to bed. When he calls again, answer, ‘Speak, Yahweh, for your servant hears you.’” And Samuel went back to his bed.
Yahweh then came and took his place there. As before he called, “Samuel! Samuel!” “Speak,” said Samuel. “Your servant hears you.”
Yahweh told Samuel, “Listen, I am going to act in Israel in a way that will leave everyone who hears of it stunned.
On that day I will bring down on Eli all that I have said about his family, from the first thing to the last.
I warned him that I would punish his family permanently for the wrong he knew about. His sons were bringing a curse on themselves,{d} and he never held them back.
So I have sworn to Eli’s family that no sacrifice or offering will ever wipe away the guilt of his house.”
Samuel lay in bed till morning. Then he opened the doors of Yahweh’s house, afraid to tell Eli what he had seen.
But Eli called him: “Samuel, my son.” “I am here,” Samuel said.
“What was the message?” Eli asked. “Do not hide it from me. May God strike you hard and then harder if you keep back one word he told you.”
So Samuel told Eli all of it, keeping nothing back. “He is Yahweh,” Eli said. “Let him do as he sees fit.”
Samuel grew, and Yahweh stayed with him. He never let one of Samuel’s words go unfulfilled.{e}
All Israel, from Dan to Beersheba,{f} knew that Samuel was truly a prophet of Yahweh.
Yahweh kept appearing at Shiloh. There he showed himself to Samuel by speaking his word.{g}

notes.text: Literally “vision was not breaking through.” The Greek Old Testament reads “there was no clear vision.”
That is, it was still night, before dawn. The lamp in the holy place burned from evening to morning (Exodus 27:20-21; Leviticus 24:2-3).
The Greek Old Testament reads “called, Samuel, Samuel.” Compare verse 10.

So the standard Hebrew text, “were cursing themselves” or “were treating it lightly.” The Greek Old Testament reads “his sons spoke evil against God.” Jewish tradition says scribes changed “God” here to avoid writing that anyone cursed him. Many scholars think “cursing God” was the first reading.
That is, everything Samuel said came true.
Dan is in the far north and Beersheba in the south. The phrase means the whole land.
The Greek Old Testament adds a longer sentence here, saying that all Israel trusted Samuel as a prophet, and that Eli was very old while his sons kept on doing wrong. Part of it may belong with 4:1.

verses.text: Samuel’s word went out to all Israel. Around then Israel went to war against the Philistines.{a} Their army set up camp near Ebenezer.{b} The Philistine army was camped farther off, at Aphek.
The Philistine soldiers took their positions facing Israel. When the fighting grew wide, Israel lost. About four thousand of their men lay dead in the field.

Back in camp, Israel’s elders asked, “Why did Yahweh let the Philistines beat us today? Let us fetch the chest of Yahweh’s covenant from Shiloh. When it is among us, it will rescue us from our enemies.”
Men went to Shiloh and carried back the chest of the covenant of Yahweh of Armies, who is enthroned above the winged creatures.{c} Eli’s sons Hophni and Phinehas walked beside God’s covenant chest.
When the chest of Yahweh’s covenant arrived in the camp, all the Israelites let out a roar so loud that the ground shook.
The Philistines heard the roar. “What is all this shouting in the Hebrew camp?” they asked. Then they found out that Yahweh’s chest had come into the camp,
They were frightened. “Their god has come into the camp!”{d} they said. “Doom is on us. Nothing like this has happened before.
Who will rescue us from gods this mighty? They are the gods who struck Egypt with all sorts of plagues in the wilderness.{e}
Be strong, Philistines, and fight like men, or you will be the Hebrews’ slaves, just as they were yours. Fight like men!”
The Philistines fought hard and beat Israel. The Israelites ran for home, every man to his own tent. It was a terrible loss. Thirty thousand Israelite foot soldiers died.
God’s chest was captured. Eli’s two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, died.
That same day a man from Benjamin ran from the battle line to Shiloh. His clothes were ripped and he had dirt on his head.{f}
Eli sat on his seat at the roadside, watching,{g} because he worried about the chest of God. When the man reached the town and spoke, the whole place cried out.
Eli heard the crying. “What is that noise?” he asked. The man rushed up and told him.
Eli was ninety-eight years old,{h} and his eyes were so weak that he could not see.
“I have just come from the battle,” the man told him. “I ran away from the front today.” “What happened, my son?” Eli asked.
The messenger said, “Israel ran from the Philistines, and many of our soldiers have died. Your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, are dead too. And the chest of God has been taken.”
At the words “chest of God,” Eli fell over backward from his seat beside the gate. His neck snapped and he died, because he was old and heavy. For forty years he had led Israel.{i}

Phinehas’s wife, Eli’s daughter-in-law, was expecting a child very soon. News came that God’s chest was gone and that her husband and her husband’s father were dead. Pains struck her suddenly, and she crouched down and gave birth.
As her life slipped away, the women standing around her said, “Take heart. You have a boy.” She gave no answer and did not seem to hear.
The baby she named Ichabod.{j} “The glory has left Israel,” she said. She said it because God’s chest was captured and because of her husband and his father.
“Israel’s glory is gone,” she said, “for God’s chest has fallen into enemy hands.”

notes.text: The Greek Old Testament begins, “In those days the Philistines gathered to fight Israel, and Israel went out to meet them.”
Ebenezer means “stone of help.” The place gets this name in 7:12. The writer uses the name his readers knew.
The winged creatures (cherubim) stood over the cover of the chest (Exodus 25:18-22). They were pictured as the throne of the unseen God.
Or “gods have come into the camp.” The Greek Old Testament reads “These are the gods who have come to them in the camp.”
Or “with every kind of plague and in the desert.” The Philistines have the story of the exodus mixed up. This may be on purpose.
Ripped clothes and dirt on the head were signs of grief and disaster.
So the traditional reading. The written Hebrew is unclear. The Greek Old Testament reads “on the seat by the gate, looking down the road.”
The Greek Old Testament reads “ninety years old.”
The Greek Old Testament reads “twenty years.”
Ichabod is usually explained as “Where is the glory?” or “No glory.” The Greek Old Testament has a different form that may mean “Woe for the glory.”

verses.text: After the Philistines captured God’s chest, they hauled it from Ebenezer to the town of Ashdod.{a}
Inside Dagon’s temple{b} they set it down by the statue of Dagon.
When Ashdod’s people got up the next day, Dagon was lying on his face on the floor before Yahweh’s chest. They stood him up and returned him to his spot.
On the following morning the same thing happened. Dagon lay on his face before Yahweh’s chest, with his head and both hands snapped off and lying at the entrance. Just his body{c} remained.
To this day, because of that, neither Dagon’s priests nor anyone else going into his temple at Ashdod will tread on that entrance.
Yahweh’s hand came down hard on the people of Ashdod. He ruined them and struck them with growths{d} all over Ashdod and the land around it.
When the men of Ashdod saw all this, they said, “Israel’s God and his chest must not stay with us. He is pressing hard on us and on Dagon, our god.”

They called together every Philistine ruler{e} and asked, “What are we to do about Israel’s God and his chest?” The rulers answered, “Take the chest of Israel’s God to Gath.” So they carried it there.
After they moved it, Yahweh’s hand came against that town and caused great panic. He struck down the people there, young and old, with growths.
Then they sent God’s chest on to Ekron. As soon as it came in, the people of Ekron screamed, “They have brought the chest of Israel’s God to us to kill us and our people!”

They again summoned all the Philistine rulers. “Send Israel’s God’s chest away,” they begged. “Let it return home, or it will destroy us and our people.” Deadly panic filled the town, for God’s hand weighed down on it.
The men who did not die were struck with growths, and the town’s cry for help went up to the sky.

notes.text: Ashdod, Gath and Ekron (verses 8-10), along with Gaza and Ashkelon, were the five main Philistine towns (6:17).
Dagon was a grain god of the peoples of that region, worshiped by the Philistines (Judges 16:23). The name probably comes from dagan, “grain.”
So the Greek Old Testament, “trunk.” The standard Hebrew text reads “only Dagon was left on him.”
Hebrew ophalim, probably swellings or boils. They may be the lumps of the plague. The Greek Old Testament adds that mice came up in the land.
Hebrew seren, a title used only for Philistine rulers.

verses.text: Yahweh’s chest stayed in Philistine country for seven months.{a}
Then the Philistines called for their priests and fortune-tellers. “What should we do with Yahweh’s chest?” they asked. “Tell us how to send it home.”

They answered, “If you send back the chest of Israel’s God, do not send it empty. You must give him a gift to make up for the wrong.{b} Then you will be healed, and you will find out why his hand has not left you.”
“What gift should we send?” they asked. The priests said, “Five gold growths and five gold mice, one for each Philistine ruler. The same plague hit you and your rulers.
Make models of your growths and of the mice that are ruining your land. Show respect to the God of Israel. Maybe he will ease up on you, on your gods, and on your land.
Do not harden your hearts as Egypt and Pharaoh did. Once God had punished them hard, they let Israel go, and Israel left.
Now build a new cart. Choose two cows with calves that have never been under a yoke. Tie the cows to the cart, but keep their calves back at the barn.
Put Yahweh’s chest on the cart. Put the gold gifts in a box next to it. Then send it on its way.

Watch what happens. If it goes up the road to Israel’s own land, toward Beth-shemesh,{c} then Yahweh sent this great trouble on us. If it does not, we will know that his hand did not hit us. It was only luck.”
The men did this. They took two nursing cows, hitched them to the cart, and shut up the calves at home.
They set Yahweh’s chest on the cart, with the box that held the gold mice and the copies of the growths.
The cows set off straight for Beth-shemesh. They kept to one road, mooing as they pulled, and never veered. The Philistine rulers walked behind them to the edge of Beth-shemesh territory.
The people of Beth-shemesh were cutting wheat in the valley.{d} They looked up, saw the chest, and were thrilled.
The cart came to the field of a man named Joshua from Beth-shemesh and stopped by a big rock. The people split up the wood of the cart and burned the cows as an offering to Yahweh.
The Levites took down Yahweh’s chest and the box with the gold gifts, and put them on the big rock. That day the men of Beth-shemesh gave burnt offerings and other sacrifices to Yahweh.
The five rulers watched this and went back to Ekron that very day.
These gold growths were the Philistines’ guilt gift to Yahweh, one for Ashdod, Gaza, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron each.

The gold mice matched the number of Philistine towns that belonged to the five rulers, both walled towns and country villages. The big rock{e} where they set down Yahweh’s chest is still there in the field of Joshua of Beth-shemesh.
But God struck down some of the people of Beth-shemesh, because they looked inside Yahweh’s chest. He killed seventy of them.{f} The people mourned because Yahweh had hit them so hard.
The men of Beth-shemesh said, “Who can stand before Yahweh, this holy God? Where can the chest go from here, away from us?”
They sent word to the people of Kiriath-jearim:{g} “The Philistines have given Yahweh’s chest back. Come down and bring it up to your place.”

notes.text: The Greek Old Testament adds, “and their land swarmed with mice.”
Hebrew asham, a gift that makes up for a wrong (Leviticus 5:14-6:7).
Beth-shemesh means “house of the sun.” It was in Israelite land, about 15 miles (24 kilometers) west of Jerusalem.
The wheat harvest came in May-June.
So some Hebrew copies and the Greek Old Testament, “the great stone.” The standard Hebrew text reads “Abel,” which may mean “meadow” or “mourning.”
So some Hebrew copies. Most Hebrew copies read “seventy men, fifty thousand men.” The larger number was probably added later.
Kiriath-jearim means “town of forests.” It was about 9 miles (14 kilometers) west of Jerusalem.

subheads.1: The Philistines Send the Chest Back

verses.text: The people of Kiriath-jearim came for Yahweh’s chest. They carried it to the home of Abinadab,{a} up on the hill, and set his son Eleazar apart to guard it.
Years dragged on while the chest stayed in Kiriath-jearim, twenty of them. During that span all Israel’s people mourned{b} for Yahweh.

Samuel addressed all of Israel. “Do you really want to return to Yahweh wholeheartedly? Then get rid of the alien gods and the Ashtoreths.{c} Fix your hearts on Yahweh and worship nobody but him. He will rescue you out of Philistine hands.”
The Israelites threw out their Baals{d} and Ashtoreths and served Yahweh only.
“Call all Israel to Mizpah,”{e} Samuel said, “and I will pray to Yahweh for you.”

They met at Mizpah. They drew water and poured it out on the ground in front of Yahweh. They went without food all day and said, “We have sinned against Yahweh.” There at Mizpah, Samuel became Israel’s judge.
News reached the Philistines that Israel had assembled at Mizpah, so their rulers marched up against them. Israel’s people got word of it and trembled.
“Keep calling out to Yahweh our God on our behalf,” they begged Samuel. “May he save us from Philistine power.”
Samuel took a young lamb that was still nursing and burned all of it as an offering to Yahweh. He prayed to Yahweh for Israel, and Yahweh answered him.
As Samuel was making the offering, the Philistines came close to attack Israel. But that very day Yahweh sent loud thunder against them. They panicked, and Israel drove them off.
Out of Mizpah the men of Israel rushed in pursuit. They cut the Philistines down until they were below Beth-car.{f}
Samuel lifted a stone and stood it upright between Mizpah and Shen.{g} “Yahweh has helped us thus far,” he said, and he called the stone Ebenezer.{h}
The Philistines were put down. They never again came into Israel’s land, because Yahweh’s hand was against them as long as Samuel lived.
Israel got back the towns that Philistines had seized, everything from Ekron as far as Gath, and the farmland round about as well. Peace also held between Israel and the Amorites.
Samuel’s judging of Israel lasted his whole life.
Every year he made a round trip through Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah, hearing Israel’s cases at each.
Then he went back to Ramah, his home. He judged Israel there too, and he built an altar to Yahweh.

notes.text: Abinadab means “my father is generous.” Eleazar means “God has helped.”
Or “mourned.” The Hebrew word is uncertain. The Greek Old Testament reads “all the house of Israel looked to the Lord.”
Ashtoreth (plural Ashtaroth) was a Canaanite goddess of love and war. The Greeks called her Astarte.
Baal, “lord” or “owner,” was the Canaanite storm god. The plural means his local forms and images.
Mizpah means “watchtower.” This Mizpah was in Benjamin, about 8 miles (13 kilometers) north of Jerusalem.
Beth-car means “house of the lamb” or “house of pasture.” The place is not known.
Shen means “tooth,” perhaps a rocky peak. The Greek Old Testament reads “the old town,” which suggests the Hebrew name Jeshanah (2 Chronicles 13:19).
Ebenezer means “stone of help.”

verses.text: When Samuel grew old, he put his sons in charge as Israel’s judges.
The older son was Joel.{a} The younger was Abijah.{b} They served as judges in Beersheba.
But the sons did not follow their father’s way. They chased after money, took bribes, and twisted the law.
So all the elders of Israel met and came to Samuel at Ramah.
“Look, you are old,” they said, “and your sons do not live the way you do. Give us a king to govern us, as other nations have.”
Samuel did not like their asking for a king to rule them. He prayed to Yahweh.
Yahweh told him, “Listen to everything the people tell you. It is not you they refuse. They refuse me, so that I will not be their king.
Since the day I led them up from Egypt they have abandoned me for other gods, again and again. Now they treat you that way.
So do as they ask. But give them a stern warning, and tell them how the king who rules over them will act.”{c}
Samuel repeated everything Yahweh had said to the people who wanted a king.
“This is what a king will do to you,” he said. “Your sons he will draft. Some must drive his chariots, some ride his horses, and some jog ahead of his chariots.
Some he will make commanders of a thousand men or of fifty. Others will have to plow his ground, bring in his crops, or make his weapons and the gear for his carts.
Your daughters he will take to mix perfume, cook, and bake.
He will seize your best fields, vineyards, and olive groves and give them to his servants.
A tenth of your grain and grapes he will collect and pass on to his officers{d} and attendants.
Your slaves, both men and women, your best young men,{e} and your donkeys he will take for his own jobs.
One sheep or goat in ten will be his. You yourselves will end up as his slaves.
Then you will cry out in protest over the king you picked. Yahweh will give you no reply that day.”
The people would not hear Samuel out. “No,” they shouted. “A king is what we need over us.
We will be like every other nation. Our own king will govern us, march in front, and fight our battles.”
Samuel listened to all that the people said and then repeated it to Yahweh.
“Do what they say,” Yahweh told Samuel. “Give them a king.” Then Samuel said to the men of Israel, “Go home, all of you, to your own towns.”

notes.text: Joel means “Yahweh is God.”
Abijah means “my father is Yahweh.”
Hebrew mishpat, “judgment, custom.” Here it means the king’s way of doing things and what he will claim from the people. Compare Deuteronomy 17:14-20.
Hebrew saris, often “eunuch,” but also used more widely for a court officer.
So the standard Hebrew text. The Greek Old Testament reads “your good herds.”

verses.text: Kish{a} was a Benjaminite, a rich and important man.{b} His father was Abiel. His grandfather was Zeror, and the family went back through Becorath to Aphiah, also of Benjamin.
Kish had a son, Saul.{c} He was a fine-looking young man. No one in Israel looked better, and he was a head taller than any of them.
One day the donkeys of Saul’s father Kish strayed. “Take a servant with you,” Kish told his son Saul, “and search for them.”

Saul and his servant passed through the hills of Ephraim and Shalishah{d} with no luck. Then they tried Shaalim, which was empty of donkeys too. Next was Benjamin’s territory, where they again came up empty.
Reaching Zuph, Saul spoke to his servant. “Come on, we should head home. Soon my father will forget the donkeys and begin to fret over the two of us.”
“Hold on,” the servant replied. “A man of God lives in this town, and everyone honors him. Whatever he predicts happens. Why not go to him? He may show us the way we should take.”
“Suppose we go,” said Saul. “What gift would we bring? Our bags have no more bread. We have nothing at all to offer God’s man.”
“I do have something,” the servant told him. “A quarter of a silver shekel, about a tenth of an ounce.{e} I can hand that to the man of God, and he will point us the right way.”
(In earlier days in Israel, a man going to ask God something would say, “Come, let us go to the seer.” Today’s prophet{f} was called a seer then.)
“A fine plan,” said Saul. “Let us go.” So the pair set out for the town of the man of God.
Climbing the slope toward the town, they ran into young women heading out for water. “Is the seer in town?” the men asked.
“He is,” the young women said. “Straight ahead. You must hurry, since he got here today. A sacrifice is being held for the people at the high place{g} this very day.

Right after you enter town you will catch him, before he walks up to eat at the high place. Nobody can begin the meal until he arrives, for he blesses the sacrifice first. Then the guests eat. Go now, and you will find him quickly.”
So up they went. Just as they walked into the town, there was Samuel, heading their way on the road up to the high place.
The previous day Yahweh had given Samuel a private message:{h}

“Tomorrow at about this hour a man from Benjamin’s land will come to you. Pour oil on him as ruler{i} over my people Israel. He will free them from Philistine control. I have noticed my people’s suffering,{j} and their cries have come to me.”
Samuel spotted Saul, and Yahweh told him, “There he is, the man I mentioned. He is the one who will rule my people.”{k}
Saul went up to Samuel by the town gate. “Could you show me the seer’s house?” he asked.
“I am the seer,” Samuel said. “Walk up to the high place before me, because you two are dining with me today. Tomorrow morning I will let you leave and answer everything you are wondering about.
Forget those donkeys that went missing three days ago. They are found. Anyway, whom does Israel desire most? You, and all of your father’s family.”
“But I belong to Benjamin, the tiniest tribe of Israel,” Saul replied. “And my clan is the lowliest in Benjamin. Why would you speak to me like this?”
Samuel led Saul and his servant to the dining hall and gave them the places of honor among the thirty or so guests.{l}
Then Samuel told the cook, “Serve the portion I handed you earlier, the one I asked you to keep aside.”

The cook took up the leg, with the meat on it,{m} and placed it before Saul. “This is what was kept back,” Samuel said. “Eat it. It has been saved for you for this occasion, ever since I said, ‘I have guests coming.’”{n} So Saul had his meal with Samuel that day.
Once they were down from the high place and back in town, Samuel spoke with Saul up on the roof.{o}
At first light they rose. Samuel called up to Saul on the roof, “Wake up! I want to see you off.” Saul rose, and both men walked outside.
Near the edge of town Samuel said, “Have your servant walk ahead of us.” The servant did. “Now stay here with me a moment,” Samuel added. “I want you to hear God’s message.”

notes.text: Kish may mean “gift” or “bow.” The meaning is uncertain. The Greek Old Testament spells the names in this family line differently.
Or “a mighty warrior.” Hebrew gibbor hayil can mean wealth, strength, or high standing.
Saul (Hebrew Shaul) means “asked for” (see 1:20 and 8:10).
The places Shalishah and Shaalim, and Zuph in verse 5, are not known.
Hebrew “a quarter of a shekel of silver,” about 0.1 ounce (3 grams). There were no coins yet, so the silver would have been weighed.
Hebrew navi. The word for seer is roeh, “one who sees.”
Hebrew bamah, a raised place of worship, often on a hill.
Literally “had uncovered Samuel’s ear.”
Hebrew nagid, “leader” or “prince.” It was a title for someone God chose to rule. It is used here in place of “king.”
So the standard Hebrew text. The Greek Old Testament reads “I have seen the low state of my people.” Compare Exodus 3:7.
Or “will rule.” The Hebrew verb usually means “hold back.”
The Greek Old Testament reads “about seventy men.”
Or “the leg and the fat tail.” The Hebrew is unclear.
The Hebrew is unclear. The Greek Old Testament reads “for it is set before you as a witness more than the others. Take some.”
So the standard Hebrew text. The Greek Old Testament reads “and they made a bed for Saul on the roof, and he lay down.” Roofs were flat and used as living space.

verses.text: Samuel lifted a flask of olive oil and tipped it over Saul’s head. Then he kissed him. “Has Yahweh not chosen you to lead his own people?{a}

Today, right after you leave me, you will meet two men beside Rachel’s tomb at Zelzah,{b} on Benjamin’s border. They will tell you, ‘Those donkeys you went to find have turned up. Your father has quit thinking about them. Now he worries about you and keeps asking, “What can I do about my son?”’

Walk on from that spot to the big tree{c} at Tabor. Three men heading to Bethel to worship God will approach you there. One drives three young goats, one brings three loaves, and one carries a wineskin.
They will greet you and offer two loaves. Take them.

After that you will arrive at Gibeath-elohim,{d} where the Philistines have a guard post.{e} As you come to the town, a group of prophets will meet you, coming down from the high place. In front of them will be lyres, drums, flutes, and harps, and they will be prophesying.
Yahweh’s Spirit will seize you, and you will prophesy together with them. You will turn into somebody new.
When these signs have happened, act as you see fit, because God is with you.
Now precede me to Gilgal.{f} I will meet you and present burnt offerings and peace offerings. Stay seven days, till I arrive with instructions for you.”
As Saul turned away from Samuel, God gave him a new heart. Every one of the signs came true that same day.
Saul and his servant reached the hill, and there a company of prophets came toward him. The Spirit of God took hold of Saul, and he joined their prophesying.
Folks who knew Saul from before watched him prophesy among the prophets. “Whatever has happened to Kish’s boy?” they said to each other. “Is even Saul among the prophets?”
A local man answered, “And who is the father of these prophets?”{g} That is how the saying began: “Is Saul among the prophets too?”
Once his prophesying ended, Saul went on to the high place.
An uncle of Saul’s said to him and the servant, “Where did you two go?” “To hunt for the donkeys,” Saul said. “They were nowhere, so we visited Samuel.”
“Do tell me,” said the uncle, “what Samuel told you.”
“He told us for sure that the donkeys were found,” Saul said. But he did not mention to his uncle the matter of the kingdom that Samuel had talked about.
Samuel summoned the people to Yahweh at Mizpah.
He told the Israelites, “Yahweh, Israel’s God, says: ‘I brought Israel up out of Egypt. I saved you from Egypt’s power and from every kingdom that mistreated you.’

But now you have turned away from your God, who rescues you from every disaster and hardship. You said,{h} ‘No! Put a king over us.’ So come stand before Yahweh, tribe by tribe and group by group.”{i}
Samuel had each tribe of Israel come forward, and the lot fell on the tribe of Benjamin.
He had Benjamin’s families come forward, and the lot fell on the family of the Matrites. Then it fell on Saul, Kish’s son.{j} They searched for Saul, but he was nowhere to be seen.
So they asked Yahweh again, “Has he come yet?”{k} Yahweh said, “He is hiding among the supplies.”
They ran and pulled him out. Standing among the people, he was a head taller than all of them.
“Here is the man Yahweh picked,” Samuel told them all. “There is nobody like him anywhere among you.” The people yelled, “May the king live!”
Samuel told the people how a king should rule,{l} and he wrote it in a book and set the book down before Yahweh. Then he sent everyone back home.
Saul went to his home in Gibeah. A band of strong men{m} went with him, men whose hearts God had stirred.

But a few troublemakers{n} sneered, “How is this fellow going to save us?” They looked down on him and brought him no gifts. Saul said nothing.{o} [Nahash, king of the Ammonites, had been brutal to the tribes of Gad and Reuben. He gouged out the right eye of each man and let no one come to Israel’s aid. Not a man east of the Jordan was left with his right eye, except seven thousand who got away from the Ammonites and fled to Jabesh-gilead.]{p}

notes.text: The Greek Old Testament has a longer text: “Has the Lord not anointed you ruler over his people Israel? You will rule the Lord’s people and save them from their enemies. This is your sign that the Lord has anointed you over his inheritance.” The standard Hebrew text probably lost the middle part when a scribe’s eye jumped from one “anointed you” to the next.
Zelzah is not known elsewhere. The Greek Old Testament reads differently.
Or “terebinth tree.”
Gibeath-elohim means “hill of God.”
Or “a garrison commander” or “a pillar.” The Hebrew word is netsib. The Greek Old Testament takes it as a name, “Nasib the Philistine.”
Gilgal means “circle” (of stones). It was near Jericho (Joshua 4:19-20).
The point is that a prophet’s calling is not handed down in a family. Anyone can receive the Spirit. The Greek Old Testament reads “And who is his father?”
So many Hebrew copies and the Greek Old Testament. The standard Hebrew text reads “you said to him,” using a word that sounds like “no.”
Or “by your clans.” The Hebrew word eleph, “thousand,” can also mean a clan or army unit.
The Greek Old Testament adds that they brought the family of Matri forward man by man. That step seems to have dropped out of the Hebrew.
So the standard Hebrew text. The Greek Old Testament reads “Will the man come here?”
Or “the custom of the kingdom.” Hebrew mishpat hammelukah. Compare 8:9-11 and Deuteronomy 17:14-20.
Hebrew “the force” or “the brave men.” The Greek Old Testament reads “sons of strength,” that is, warriors.
Hebrew “sons of Belial.”

So the standard Hebrew text, literally “and he was like one keeping silent.” With a small change in the Hebrew letters, the Dead Sea Scroll 4QSam-a and the Greek Old Testament read “About a month later,” which begins chapter 11.

The bracketed paragraph appears in the Dead Sea Scroll 4QSam-a, a Hebrew copy of Samuel from Qumran (first century BC), between 10:27 and 11:1. It is not in the standard Hebrew text or the Greek Old Testament, but the ancient writer Josephus tells the same story. Many scholars think the standard Hebrew text lost it by a copying error. Others think it was added to explain Nahash’s demand in 11:2. The scroll is damaged in places, and this wording is this translation’s own.

verses.text: Nahash{a} the Ammonite came up and laid siege to Jabesh-gilead.{b} The men of Jabesh begged him, “Sign a treaty with us, and we will work for you.”
Nahash replied, “Here is my one condition for a treaty. I will poke out everyone’s right eye. This will bring shame on the whole nation of Israel.”
Jabesh’s elders said, “Let us have a week. We will send word through the whole country. When nobody comes to save us, we will give up to you.”
The messengers reached Saul’s town, Gibeah, and told the news to the people. They all burst into loud weeping.
Saul happened to be returning from the fields, driving his oxen. “What is the matter?” he asked. “Why are the people sobbing?” They repeated the words of the men of Jabesh.
When Saul heard it, God’s Spirit came on him with power, and he became furious.

He grabbed a team of oxen, cut them to bits, and had messengers carry the bits through every part of Israel. “Whoever fails to come out after Saul and Samuel,” they said, “will find his own oxen treated this way!” Dread from Yahweh came over the people, and they marched out united.
At Bezek Saul took a count. Israel had three hundred thousand soldiers and Judah thirty thousand.{c}
To the messengers he said, “Tell the people of Jabesh-gilead that help comes tomorrow, when the sun is high and hot.” The messengers carried this back, and Jabesh rejoiced.
The men of Jabesh told the Ammonites, “Tomorrow we will give ourselves up to you. Do with us whatever seems good to you.”

Early next day Saul split his men into three groups. They rushed into the Ammonite camp in the last part of the night{d} and killed them until the day grew hot. The few who survived were so scattered that no two stayed together.
The people said to Samuel, “Who asked, ‘Will Saul be our king?’ Bring those men here and we will kill them.”
“Nobody will be killed today,” Saul said. “This is the day Yahweh saved Israel.”
Samuel told the people, “Let us go to Gilgal and make Saul king again.”
The whole people went to Gilgal. Before Yahweh they crowned Saul king.{e} They offered peace offerings to Yahweh, and Saul and all of Israel held a huge celebration.

notes.text: Nahash means “snake.” Some old copies put the paragraph from 10:27 before this verse (see the note there). The Greek Old Testament and the Dead Sea Scroll 4QSam-a begin this verse “About a month later.”
Jabesh-gilead was a town east of the Jordan, in Gilead. Jabesh means “dry.” Compare Judges 21:8-14.
The Greek Old Testament reads “six hundred thousand” and “seventy thousand.” The Hebrew word eleph, “thousand,” may also mean an army unit, which would make the numbers far smaller.
Hebrew “in the morning watch,” the last of the three night watches, from about 2 a.m. to about 6 a.m.
The Greek Old Testament reads “and Samuel anointed Saul king there before the Lord,” and ends the verse “and Samuel and all Israel were very glad.”

verses.text: Samuel told all Israel, “I have done everything you asked of me. I gave you a king.
Now the king leads you. I am old, with gray hair, and my sons are here among you. I have led you from the time I was young until now.

Here I am. Speak against me in front of Yahweh and his anointed king. Did I ever take someone’s ox or donkey? Did I cheat anyone or abuse anyone? Did I accept a bribe to look the other way?{a} If so, tell me and I will pay it back.”
“You never cheated us or abused us,” they answered. “You never took a thing from any person.”
“Yahweh is witness against you,” he said to them, “and so is his anointed king today, that nothing was found in my hands.” “Yes, witness,” they said.{b}
Samuel told the people, “Yahweh is the witness.{c} He appointed Moses and Aaron, and he led your ancestors up from Egypt.
Now stand here. I will state my case against you before Yahweh, going over every just act Yahweh did for you and your ancestors.
After Jacob arrived in Egypt,{d} your ancestors called out to Yahweh. He sent Moses and Aaron, who took them from Egypt and made them live in this land.
They forgot Yahweh their God. So he let them fall into the power of Sisera, who commanded the army of Hazor,{e} and the Philistines, and the king of Moab. All of them fought against Israel.
They called to Yahweh, ‘We have sinned. We left Yahweh and served the Baals and Ashtoreths. Rescue us from the enemies who attack us, and serving you will be our work.’
Yahweh sent Jerubbaal,{f} Bedan,{g} Jephthah, and Samuel,{h} and he saved you from enemies all around. You lived safely.
Then Nahash, the Ammonite king, advanced against you. You answered, ‘Never! We want a king for ourselves,’ though Yahweh your God was your king.
So here is the king you chose and asked for. Yahweh has put a king over you.
If you honor Yahweh, serve him, listen to him, and obey his orders, and if you and your king both follow Yahweh your God, you will be fine.{i}
But if you disobey Yahweh and defy his orders, Yahweh’s hand will fall on you, as it fell on your ancestors.{j}
Now stand still and watch the great thing Yahweh is about to do in front of you.
Surely it is wheat harvest season?{k} I will pray to Yahweh. He will send thunder and rain. And you will realize what a serious wrong you did in Yahweh’s eyes when you demanded a king.”
Samuel called to Yahweh, and that same day Yahweh sent thunder and rain. All the people were afraid of Yahweh and of Samuel.
“Pray to Yahweh your God for us, your servants,” they said to Samuel. “We do not want to die. On top of all our other sins, we have done this evil thing by asking for a king.”
“Do not be afraid,” Samuel said. “You really have done all this evil. But do not stop following Yahweh. Serve him with all your heart.
Do not follow useless idols.{l} They cannot help you or save you. They are useless.
For the sake of his great name, Yahweh will not leave his people, because he chose to make you his own.
For my part, I will never sin against Yahweh by giving up on prayer for you. I will instruct you in the right and good path.
Only honor Yahweh. Serve him with true loyalty and all your heart, and think of the great deeds he has done for you.
But if you keep on doing evil, you and your king will both be swept away.”

notes.text: So the standard Hebrew text. The Greek Old Testament reads “a bribe, even a sandal? Testify against me.” Sirach 46:19 seems to have a similar text.
So many Hebrew copies and the Greek Old Testament. The standard Hebrew text reads “he said.”
“Is the witness” is added from the Greek Old Testament. The Hebrew does not have the words.
The Greek Old Testament adds “and his sons, and Egypt made them low.”
The Greek Old Testament reads “Sisera, commander of the army of Jabin king of Hazor.”
Jerubbaal is another name for Gideon (Judges 6:32).
So the standard Hebrew text. Bedan is not named in Judges. The Greek Old Testament reads “Barak,” which fits Judges 4-5.
So the standard Hebrew text. Some ancient copies, such as the Syriac, are reported to read “Samson.”
“Things will go well” is added. The Hebrew sentence stops after “your God.”
Literally “against you and against your ancestors,” as in the standard Hebrew text. The Greek Old Testament reads “against you and against your king.”
The wheat harvest was in May or June, the dry season, when rain almost never fell.
Hebrew tohu, “emptiness,” the word used in Genesis 1:2 (“formless”).

verses.text: Saul was [...] years old when he began his rule, and he ruled over Israel for [...] two years.{a}

Saul picked three thousand Israelite men. Two thousand stayed with him at Michmash{b} and in the Bethel hills. A thousand were with his son Jonathan{c} at Gibeah in Benjamin. He told all the other men to go home.
Jonathan attacked the Philistine post{d} at Geba, and the Philistines heard of it. Saul had trumpets blown across the land. “Let the Hebrews hear this!” he said.{e}
All Israel heard that Saul had attacked the Philistine post and that the Philistines now hated Israel. The people were summoned to join Saul at Gilgal.

A huge Philistine force gathered to fight Israel: thirty thousand chariots,{f} six thousand horsemen, and warriors beyond number, like sand along the sea. They marched up and made camp at Michmash, east of Beth-aven.{g}
The Israelites could see they were in a tight spot, with the enemy pressing hard. Some hid in caves, in thorn bushes, among rocks, in pits,{h} and in wells.
Some Hebrews fled across the Jordan into the lands of Gad and Gilead. Saul stayed at Gilgal, and his army shook with fear as it followed him.
Saul waited the seven days Samuel had set. Samuel did not show up at Gilgal, and Saul’s men began slipping away.
“Hand me the burnt offering and the peace offerings,” Saul ordered. Then he offered the burnt offering himself.
Hardly had the burnt offering ended when Samuel appeared. Saul walked out to greet him.{i}
“What have you done?” Samuel asked. “My men were deserting,” Saul replied. “You had not come by the day you named. And the Philistines were mustering at Michmash.
I told myself, ‘Philistines are about to attack me at Gilgal, and I have not yet begged Yahweh’s favor.’ So I felt forced to present the burnt offering.”
“That was foolish,” Samuel said. “You did not keep the order your God Yahweh gave you. If you had, Yahweh would have made your rule over Israel last forever.
As it is, your rule will not continue. Yahweh has found a man who pleases his heart. Yahweh has named him leader of his people, because you did not do what Yahweh ordered.”
Samuel left Gilgal and climbed to Gibeah of Benjamin.{j} Saul counted the men who remained with him. They numbered about six hundred.
Geba in Benjamin was where Saul, his son Jonathan, and their men were staying. The Philistines had their camp at Michmash.
Out of the Philistine camp came raiders in three groups. One group headed along the Ophrah road toward Shual.
A second took the Beth-horon road. The third took the road along the border, above the Valley of Zeboim,{k} facing the wilderness.
In all Israel there was not a single metalworker. The Philistines had decided, “The Hebrews might forge swords or spears.”
So Israelites had to go to the Philistines to get plow points, hoes, axes, or sickles sharpened.{l}
The fee was about a quarter of an ounce of silver{m} for plow points and hoes, and about an eighth of an ounce{n} for sharpening forks and axes and for fixing ox prods.
So when the battle came, no soldier with Saul or Jonathan had a sword or spear. Only Saul and Jonathan had them.
A Philistine detachment moved out toward the Michmash pass.

notes.text: The Hebrew of this verse is incomplete. Word for word it reads “Saul was a year old when he became king, and he reigned two years over Israel.” A number was lost before “year” and probably before “two years.” The verse is not in the Greek Old Testament. Acts 13:21 gives Saul’s reign as forty years. Josephus gives twenty or forty in different places. Some later Greek copies read “thirty years old.” The gaps in brackets mark the missing numbers.
Michmash was a town about 7 miles (11 kilometers) northeast of Jerusalem.
Jonathan means “Yahweh has given.”
Or “the garrison commander” or “the Philistine pillar.” Hebrew netsib. The Greek Old Testament reads “Nasib the Philistine.” Same in verse 4.
So the standard Hebrew text. The Greek Old Testament reads “The slaves have revolted,” taking the Hebrew letters another way.
So the standard Hebrew text and the Greek Old Testament. Some Greek copies and the Syriac are reported to read “three thousand,” which may be the original.
Beth-aven means “house of wickedness.” It may be a mocking name for Bethel (“house of God”). Compare Hosea 4:15.
Or “tombs” or “strongholds.” The Hebrew word is rare.
Literally “to bless him.”

So the standard Hebrew text. The Greek Old Testament has a longer text that adds that the rest of the people followed Saul to meet the soldiers coming from Gilgal to Gibeah. The Hebrew may have lost words by a copying error.
Zeboim means “hyenas.”
So the Greek Old Testament (“sickle”). The Hebrew repeats the word for “plow point.”
Hebrew pim, a weight found in digs, about two-thirds of a shekel (8 grams). The meaning of this verse was unknown until such weights were found. The Greek Old Testament reads “three shekels.”
Hebrew “a third of a shekel,” about 4 grams.

verses.text: One day Jonathan, Saul’s son, said to the young man who carried his armor, “Let us cross over to the Philistine post on the far side.” He did not tell his father.
Saul was resting at the edge of Gibeah under the pomegranate tree at Migron. About six hundred men were with him.

With them was Ahijah,{a} who wore the ephod.{b} He was a son of Ahitub, a brother of Ichabod, and a grandson of Phinehas, who was Eli’s son. Eli had been Yahweh’s priest at Shiloh. The army did not realize Jonathan was gone.
Jonathan planned to go through a pass to reach the Philistine post. Steep rock stood on either side of it. The names of the two crags were Bozez and Seneh.{c}
Bozez rose to the north, facing Michmash. Seneh rose to the south, facing Geba.
“Come,” Jonathan said to his armor-bearer. “Let us cross to the post of those pagans. Maybe Yahweh will act for us. Nothing can stop Yahweh from saving, whether he uses many men or just a few.”
“Do what you have in mind,” his armor-bearer said. “Go on. I am with you, whatever you choose.”{d}
“Then here is what we will do,” Jonathan said. “We will cross over and let the men see us.
Suppose they say, ‘Hold still until we get to you.’ Then we will stay put and not climb up.
Suppose they say, ‘Come up to us.’ Then up we go. That means Yahweh has given them to us. This is our signal.”
The two let the Philistine post see them. “Look!” the Philistines said. “Hebrews are crawling out of the holes where they hid.”

The men at the post shouted down to Jonathan and his armor-bearer, “Come up here, and we will teach you a lesson!” “Follow me up,” Jonathan told his armor-bearer. “Yahweh has handed them over to Israel.”
Jonathan scrambled up on his hands and knees, with his armor-bearer behind him. The Philistines fell before Jonathan, and the armor-bearer killed them as he came after.
That first blow brought down some twenty men, killed by Jonathan and the man carrying his armor, within an area about half an acre.{e}
Fear swept the Philistine camp, the open country, and all the troops. Even the guard post and the raiders shook. The ground trembled, and a terror from God{f} took hold.
Saul’s watchmen at Gibeah in Benjamin looked and saw the crowd breaking up and rushing in every direction.{g}
“Count the men and find out who has left us,” Saul told those with him. They counted. Jonathan and his armor-bearer were missing.
“Bring God’s chest here,” Saul said to Ahijah.{h} At that time the chest was with the Israelites.
While Saul was speaking to the priest, the noise in the Philistine camp kept getting louder. Saul said to the priest, “Stop. Put your hand down.”
Saul and all his men gathered and went to the fight. They found the Philistines swinging swords at each other, in complete chaos.
The Hebrews who had served the Philistines and gone up with them to camp now changed sides.{i} They sided with the Israelites under Saul and Jonathan.
Every Israelite hiding in Ephraim’s hill country heard the Philistines were fleeing. They also rushed out in hot pursuit.
So Yahweh saved Israel that day, and the fighting moved past Beth-aven.{j}
The Israelites were worn out that day. Saul had made the people swear an oath: “A curse on any man who eats before evening, before I get revenge on my enemies.”{k} So no one ate anything.
The whole army{l} entered a wooded area, and honey lay on the ground.
They came into the woods and saw honey dripping, but no hand went to any mouth. The oath scared them.
Jonathan, though, never heard his father put the army under oath. He pushed the tip of his staff into a honeycomb and ate some. His eyes brightened.{m}
One of the soldiers told him, “Your father made the army swear a firm oath. ‘A curse on any man who eats today,’ he said.” And the men were weak.
“My father has caused trouble for our country,” Jonathan said. “Look how bright my eyes are, just from tasting a bit of this honey.
It would have been far better if the men had eaten freely today from what they took from their enemies. The Philistines would have been struck down much harder.”
That day Israel beat the Philistines from Michmash all the way to Aijalon, and the people were exhausted.
The men leaped on the loot. They grabbed sheep, cattle, and calves, killed them right on the ground, and ate the meat with the blood still in it.
“Look,” someone told Saul, “the men are sinning against Yahweh. They are eating meat with the blood in it.” “You have broken faith,” Saul said. “Roll a big stone over here now.”{n}

“Move among the men,” he said, “and say this: ‘Every man must bring his ox or sheep to me. Slaughter it on this stone, then eat. Do not offend Yahweh by eating meat with the blood.’” That night each man led his ox over and slaughtered it there.
Saul built an altar for Yahweh. He had never built one for him before.

“Let us go after the Philistines tonight,” Saul said, “and loot them until sunrise. We will not leave one alive.” “Do whatever you think is best,” the men said. But the priest said, “First let us ask God.”
Saul inquired of God, “May I chase the Philistines? Will you give Israel the win?” But God did not reply that day.
“Step forward, all you chiefs{o} of the people,” said Saul. “Let us learn how today’s sin came about.
As surely as Yahweh lives, the one who saves Israel, the guilty one must die, even if it is my son Jonathan.” Nobody in the whole army said a word.
Addressing all Israel, Saul said, “Take your places over there. Jonathan and I will stand opposite.” “Do whatever you think right,” the people answered.
Saul prayed to Yahweh, Israel’s God, “Give Thummim.”{p} The lot fell on Jonathan and Saul, and the people were cleared.
“Now cast the lot between me and my son Jonathan,” Saul said. The lot fell on Jonathan.{q}
“Tell me what you did,” Saul said to Jonathan. “I tasted a little honey on the tip of my staff,” Jonathan said. “Here I am. I will die.”
“God do the same to me, and worse, if you do not die, Jonathan,” said Saul.

The people said to Saul, “Should Jonathan die, after bringing Israel this huge win? No way! As Yahweh lives, no hair of his head will touch the ground. God was with him today.” The people thus rescued Jonathan from death.
Saul gave up the chase, and the Philistines went home.
When Saul had secured his hold on the throne of Israel, he went to war on every side against Moab, Edom, the Ammonites, the Philistines, and the kings of Zobah. In every direction he went, he won.{r}
He fought with courage and beat the Amalekites, freeing Israel from the raiders who had been stealing from them.
Saul had three sons, named Jonathan, Ishvi,{s} and Malchi-shua.{t} His daughters were Merab, who was older, and Michal, who was younger.{u}
Saul married Ahinoam,{v} the daughter of Ahimaaz. Abner{w} commanded his army. Abner was the son of Ner, an uncle of Saul.
Saul’s father was Kish. Abner’s father was Ner, who was Abiel’s son.
Fierce fighting against the Philistines lasted all of Saul’s days. Any strong or brave man Saul came across, he recruited.

notes.text: Ahijah means “brother of Yahweh” or “Yahweh is my brother.”
Here the ephod is a priest’s garment used to seek God’s answer (compare 23:9-12).
Bozez may mean “shining” and Seneh “thorny.” Both are uncertain.
So the standard Hebrew text, word for word “Turn. Here I am with you as your heart.” The Greek Old Testament reads “my heart is as your heart.”

Hebrew “about half a furrow of a yoke of field,” probably half what a pair of oxen could plow in a day. The phrase is unclear. The Greek Old Testament reads “with darts and slings and stones of the field.” This needs scholarly review.
Or “a very great terror.”
So the standard Hebrew text, word for word “and it went and hither.” The Greek Old Testament reads “thrown into confusion on every side.”
So the standard Hebrew text. The Greek Old Testament reads “Bring the ephod,” because he wore the ephod at that time. That agrees with verses 3 and 19.
So the Greek Old Testament and other ancient copies. The Hebrew reads “who went up with them into the camp all around, they also.”
The Greek Old Testament adds that Saul had about ten thousand men and that the fighting spread through every town in the hills of Ephraim.
The Greek Old Testament begins this verse, “Saul made a great mistake of ignorance that day.”
Hebrew “all the land.” The Hebrew of verses 25-26 is hard.
So the written Hebrew text. The traditional reading is “his eyes saw clearly.”
So the standard Hebrew text. The Greek Old Testament reads “Roll a great stone to me here from Gittaim.”
Hebrew “cornerstones,” a picture of leaders.

So the standard Hebrew text, word for word “Give perfect,” where the Hebrew word may be read as Thummim. The Greek Old Testament has a longer text, in which Saul asks why God has not answered and asks whether the guilt is in him or in Jonathan. Many scholars think the Hebrew once read, “If this guilt is in me or in my son Jonathan, give Urim. If it is in your people Israel, give Thummim,” and that words dropped out by a copying error. Urim and Thummim were the sacred lots (Exodus 28:30).
The Greek Old Testament adds that whoever the Lord picks by lot must die, that the people told Saul not to do this, and that Saul gave in to them.
So the standard Hebrew text. The Greek Old Testament reads “he won,” from a Hebrew word with similar letters.
The Greek Old Testament reads “Jessiu.” Ishvi may be another name for Abinadab (31:2; 1 Chronicles 8:33) or for Ish-bosheth (2 Samuel 2:8). It may mean “man of Yahweh,” but that is uncertain.
Malchi-shua means “my king is salvation” or “king of wealth.” Both are uncertain.
Merab may mean “increase” and Michal “who is like God?” Both are uncertain.
Ahinoam means “my brother is pleasantness.”
Abner means “my father is a lamp.”

verses.text: “Yahweh sent me to pour oil on your head and make you king of his people Israel,” Samuel told Saul. “So hear Yahweh’s words now.
This is the message of Yahweh of Armies: ‘Amalek’s treatment of Israel will be punished. They stood in Israel’s path as Israel came up from Egypt.{a}
Go, attack Amalek, and place all they own under the ban.{b} Do not pity them. Put to death men, women, children, and babies, along with oxen, sheep, camels, and donkeys.’”
Saul gathered the army at Telaim{c} and numbered it: ten thousand from Judah, along with two hundred thousand on foot.{d}
Saul moved on toward the town of Amalek and set a trap in the valley.

Saul warned the Kenites, “Get away from the Amalekites, or I will wipe you out along with them. You were good to all the Israelites when they left Egypt.” So the Kenites moved off from the Amalekites.
Saul struck the Amalekites from Havilah all the way to Shur, near Egypt’s eastern border.
Agag,{e} the Amalekite king, he took alive. Everyone else he put under the ban, killing them by the sword.

Yet Saul and the soldiers spared Agag. They also saved the finest sheep and cattle, the fat ones,{f} the lambs, and all that was good. They refused to destroy these. Whatever was weak or worthless, they did destroy.
Yahweh’s word came to Samuel, saying,
“I regret making Saul king,” Yahweh said. “He has stopped following me and has ignored my orders.” This troubled Samuel,{g} and all night he called out to Yahweh.
Next morning Samuel rose to look for Saul. He heard, “Saul has gone to Carmel,{h} and there he raised a monument to himself. Afterward he moved on down to Gilgal.”{i}
Samuel reached Saul. “Yahweh bless you!” Saul said. “I have done what Yahweh told me.”
“Then what is that sound of sheep I hear?” Samuel said. “And what is that mooing of cattle?”
“The soldiers brought them from the Amalekites,” Saul said. “They kept the best sheep and cattle to sacrifice to Yahweh your God. We put the rest under the ban.”
“Stop right there,” Samuel told Saul. “I will tell you what Yahweh said to me last night.” “Tell me,” said Saul.
“Once you thought little of yourself,” Samuel said. “But you became leader of Israel’s tribes. Yahweh anointed you king over Israel.
He sent you off with orders: ‘Go and wipe out those sinners, the Amalekites. Fight them until they are finished.’
Why did you not obey Yahweh? Why did you rush on the loot and do what Yahweh calls evil?”
“But I did obey Yahweh,” Saul said to Samuel. “I went on the mission Yahweh gave me. I brought Agag the Amalekite king here, and the rest of Amalek I put under the ban.
The soldiers took sheep and cattle from the loot, the best of what was under the ban, to sacrifice to Yahweh your God at Gilgal.”
Samuel answered, “What pleases Yahweh more, burnt offerings and sacrifices, or doing what he says? Listen: obeying is better than sacrifice, and paying attention is better than the fat of rams.
Rebelling is as bad as the sin of fortune-telling. Stubbornness is as bad as idol worship.{j} You have turned down Yahweh’s word, so he has turned you down as king.”
“I have sinned,” Saul said to Samuel. “I disobeyed Yahweh’s order and yours. I feared the army, so I did what they wanted.
Forgive this sin, I beg you, and walk back with me. I want to bow down to Yahweh.”
“No, I will not return with you,” Samuel told Saul. “You rejected Yahweh’s word, and Yahweh has rejected you as Israel’s king.”
Samuel spun around to leave, and Saul{k} caught hold of his robe’s hem. It tore.
“Today Yahweh has torn Israel’s kingdom from you,” Samuel said, “and handed it to a neighbor of yours who is better than you.
Israel’s Glory{l} does not lie or change his mind. He is no human who changes his mind.”
“I have sinned,” Saul said. “Still, honor me now in the presence of my people’s elders and of all Israel. Return with me, and I will bow to Yahweh your God.”
Samuel went back with Saul, and Saul worshiped Yahweh.
“Fetch Agag the Amalekite king for me,” Samuel said. Agag came toward him in chains,{m} thinking, “Surely the worst of death is past.”{n}
“Your sword made mothers childless,” Samuel said. “Now your mother will be childless too.” And Samuel cut Agag to pieces in front of Yahweh at Gilgal.
Samuel went off to Ramah, and Saul climbed to his home at Gibeah of Saul.
To his dying day Samuel never saw Saul again, though he mourned for him. And Yahweh regretted making Saul king of Israel.

notes.text: See Exodus 17:8-16 and Deuteronomy 25:17-19.
Hebrew herem, giving people and goods to God by destroying them completely. Same in the rest of this chapter.
Telaim (“lambs”) may be the Telem of Joshua 15:24. The Greek Old Testament reads “Gilgal.”
The Greek Old Testament reads “four hundred thousand” and “thirty thousand.” On “thousand,” see the note at 11:8.
Agag may have been a royal title for Amalekite kings (compare Numbers 24:7). The meaning is uncertain.
The meaning of the Hebrew is uncertain. It may mean “the second-born” or “the fattened.”
Or “was troubled.”
This Carmel was a town in the hills of Judah, south of Hebron (compare 25:2), not Mount Carmel.
The Greek Old Testament adds that when Samuel came to Gilgal, Saul was offering a burnt offering to the Lord from the best of the loot taken from Amalek.
Hebrew teraphim. The Hebrew of this line is hard. The Greek Old Testament reads differently: “idols bring on pain and grief.”
So the Greek Old Testament and 4QSam-a (as reported). The Hebrew does not have “Saul.”
Or “the Eternal One” or “the Splendor.” Hebrew netsah.
Or “cheerfully” or “unsteadily.” The Hebrew word is uncertain. The Greek Old Testament reads “trembling.”
So the standard Hebrew text. The Greek Old Testament reads “Is death really so bitter?” A shorter Greek may reflect a Hebrew text reported to read “Surely death is bitter.”

verses.text: Yahweh said to Samuel, “How long will you keep mourning for Saul? I have turned him down as Israel’s king. Fill your horn with oil and go. I am sending you to a man named Jesse{a} in Bethlehem. One of his sons is my choice for king.”
“How can I go?” Samuel said. “Saul will hear and have me killed.” Yahweh said, “Bring a young cow and say, ‘I have come to sacrifice to Yahweh.’
Ask Jesse to the sacrifice. At that point I will tell you what to do. Pour the oil on the person I name.”
Samuel did what Yahweh said. He came to Bethlehem,{b} and the town’s elders came out to him shaking. “Do you come in peace?”{c} they asked.
“Yes, in peace,” he said. “I have come to sacrifice to Yahweh. Make yourselves clean and join me at the sacrifice.” He also made Jesse and his sons clean and invited them to the sacrifice.
When they arrived, Samuel saw Eliab.{d} He thought, “This must be the one Yahweh will anoint.”

But Yahweh said to Samuel, “Do not judge by his face or his great height. I have turned him down. Yahweh does not look at things the way people do.{e} People look at the outside.{f} Yahweh looks at the heart.”
Jesse called his son Abinadab{g} and had him walk past Samuel. “Yahweh has not picked this one either,” Samuel said.
Next Jesse had Shammah{h} walk past. “Yahweh has not picked this one either,” Samuel said.
Jesse had seven of his sons walk past Samuel. Samuel told Jesse, “Yahweh has picked none of these.”

“Are these all the boys you have?” Samuel asked. “There is still the youngest,” Jesse said. “He is out with the sheep.” “Send for him,” Samuel said. “We will not sit down to the meal{i} until he gets here.”
Jesse sent for him. The boy had a healthy, reddish glow, with fine eyes and a handsome look. “Get up and anoint him,” Yahweh said. “He is the one.”
Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed him while his brothers stood by. From then on Yahweh’s Spirit came on David{j} with power. Samuel went back to Ramah.
Yahweh’s Spirit left Saul, and a harmful spirit sent by Yahweh troubled him.{k}
Saul’s servants told him, “A harmful spirit from God is troubling you.
Master, give your servants the order. We will search for a man who plays the lyre well. Each time the harmful spirit from God descends on you, he can play, and you will feel better.”
“Look for a skilled player,” Saul told his servants, “and have him come to me.”
One of the servants spoke up. “I know a son of Jesse of Bethlehem who plays well. He is a brave fighter and a soldier, good with words and good to look at. Yahweh is with him.”
Saul sent messengers to Jesse. “Send me your son David, the shepherd,” they said.
Jesse loaded a donkey with bread,{l} a skin of wine, and a young goat, and sent David to Saul with them.
Arriving, David went to work for Saul. Saul loved him dearly, and David became one of his armor-bearers.
Saul sent word to Jesse: “Let David stay with me. I like him.”
From then on, whenever the spirit from God troubled Saul, David took his lyre and played. Saul would calm down and feel better, and the harmful spirit would go away.

notes.text: Jesse may mean “Yahweh exists” or “man.” Both are uncertain.
Bethlehem means “house of bread.”
Or “Is it peace?” The Greek Old Testament adds “you seer.”
Eliab means “my God is father.”
The Hebrew is short, word for word “for not what man sees.” The Greek Old Testament reads “for God does not see as a man looks.”
Hebrew “the eyes,” that is, how things look on the outside.
Abinadab means “my father is generous.”
Shammah may be a short form of a name meaning “Yahweh has heard.” It is uncertain. He is called Shimeah in 2 Samuel 13:3 and Shimea in 1 Chronicles 2:13.
So the Greek Old Testament. The Hebrew reads “will not turn around” or “sit around,” probably at the meal.
David may mean “beloved.” It is uncertain. This is the first time David is named.
Or “frightened him.”

Hebrew hamor, “donkey,” can also be read homer, a dry measure of about 6 bushels (220 liters). The Greek Old Testament reads “a homer of bread.” But a donkey loaded with bread is the more likely meaning.

verses.text: The Philistines massed their armies for battle at Socoh,{a} a Judean town. Their camp lay at Ephes-dammim,{b} located between Socoh and Azekah.
Saul and the Israelites came together and set up camp in the Valley of Elah.{c} They formed ranks against the Philistines.
The Philistines held the hill on one side and Israel held the hill on the other, with the valley in between.
A fighter{d} stepped out from the Philistine camp. His name was Goliath,{e} from Gath. He was nearly ten feet tall, about nine feet nine inches.{f}
A bronze helmet sat on his head. He wore scale armor that weighed about a hundred twenty-five pounds{g} of bronze.
He had bronze guards on his shins and a small bronze spear{h} hanging across his back.
His spear shaft was as thick as a weaver’s rod, and its iron point weighed about fifteen pounds.{i} His shield was carried by a man who walked ahead of him.
He stood and shouted at the Israelite battle lines, “Why have you lined up for war? I am a Philistine, and you serve Saul. Pick a man to come down against me.
Should he defeat and kill me, then we become your slaves. But should I defeat and kill him, you become our slaves and work for us.”
“Today I challenge Israel’s armies,” the Philistine added. “Give me a man to fight one on one.”
When Saul and all the Israelites heard the Philistine’s words, they were stunned and terrified.
Now David’s father was Jesse, an Ephrathite{j} from Bethlehem in Judah, a man with eight sons. By Saul’s day Jesse was elderly, far along in years.{k}
Three of Jesse’s older sons had gone to the war with Saul. They were Eliab, the firstborn, then Abinadab, then Shammah.
David was the youngest. The three oldest were with Saul,
but David kept going back and forth between Saul and Bethlehem, where he tended his father’s sheep.
For forty days, every morning and evening, the Philistine came forward and took his stand.
Jesse told his son David, “Take your brothers this basket of roasted grain, about three-fifths of a bushel,{l} and these ten loaves. Hurry to the camp.
Take these ten cheeses{m} to their commander too. Check on your brothers and see how they are. Bring back something from them to show they are well.{n}
They are with Saul and all the other Israelites in the Valley of Elah, fighting the Philistines.”
David got up early next morning, left the sheep with another shepherd, loaded up, and went as Jesse had said. He reached the camp{o} as the army was moving out to its position with a battle shout.
Israel and the Philistines lined up, each army facing the other.
David left his load with the man who guarded supplies, ran to the battle line, and greeted his brothers to ask how they were.
While he was talking with them, Goliath, the Philistine fighter from Gath, came out from the Philistine ranks and shouted his usual words. David heard him.
When the Israelites saw the man, they all ran away in great fear.

“See that man coming out?” the Israelites asked. “He comes to jeer at Israel. Whoever kills him will get a fortune from the king, who will also let him marry his daughter and cancel the taxes owed by his father’s family.{p}”
