David quizzed those beside him: “What does the man receive who kills this Philistine and removes Israel’s disgrace? Who does he think he is, this pagan, mocking the armies of the living God?”
They gave him the same news: “That is the prize for whoever kills him.”

David’s oldest brother Eliab heard David talking with the men and grew angry. “What are you doing here?” he said. “Who is looking after those few sheep in the wilderness? I know how conceited and wicked you are. You came down only to see the fight.”
“Now what have I done?” David said. “I only asked a question.”
He turned to someone else with the same question, and the men answered just as before.
Someone overheard David’s words and reported them to Saul, who sent for him.{q}
“Nobody should lose heart because of this man,”{r} David told Saul. “I will go and fight this Philistine.”
“You cannot fight him,” Saul said. “You are just a boy, and he has been a soldier since he was young.”
“I have looked after my father’s sheep,” David said. “When a lion or bear came and carried off a lamb,
I chased it, hit it, and pulled the lamb out of its mouth. When it turned on me, I grabbed its fur{s} and hit it until it was dead.
I have killed lions and bears. This pagan Philistine will end up like them, since he has mocked the armies of the living God.{t}
“The same Yahweh who saved me from lions and bears will save me from this Philistine,” David said. “Go, then, and Yahweh be with you,” said Saul.
Saul dressed David in his own clothes, put a bronze helmet on his head, and fitted a coat of armor over his body.
David strapped Saul’s sword over the clothes and tried to walk, but he had never worn such gear. “I cannot move in these,” he told Saul. He took them off.
He picked up his stick, chose five smooth stones from the creek, and put them in the pouch of his shepherd’s bag. Sling in hand, he walked toward the Philistine.
The Philistine kept coming nearer to David, with the man who carried his shield walking ahead.{u}
He looked David over and sneered. David was just a boy, with a healthy, handsome face.
“Am I a dog, that you come at me with sticks?”{v} the Philistine said. He called down curses on David in the names of his gods.
“Come here,” he said. “I will give your body to the birds and the wild animals.”
David answered, “You come at me with sword, spear, and small spear. I come at you in the name of Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel’s armies, whom you have mocked.

Today Yahweh puts you in my power. I will strike you down, and your head will come off. Today the bodies{w} of the Philistine army will be food for birds and wild animals. And every land will learn that Israel has a God.
And everyone here will know that Yahweh does not save with sword or spear. The battle is Yahweh’s, and he will give you to us.”
The Philistine moved in to attack. David ran fast toward the Philistine line to meet him.{x}
David put his hand in his bag, took out a stone, and slung it. It hit the Philistine in the forehead and sank in.{y} He fell face down on the ground.
David won over the Philistine with a sling and a single stone. He struck him down and killed him, with no sword in his hand.{z}

David ran to him and stood over him. He seized the Philistine’s sword, slid it from its sheath, and killed him by cutting off his head. The Philistines saw that their champion was dead, and they fled.
Israel and Judah’s men shouted and chased the Philistines as far as Gai{aa} and the gates of Ekron. Wounded Philistines lay along the whole road from Shaaraim{ab} to Gath and Ekron.
The Israelites headed back after the chase and plundered the Philistine camp.
The Philistine’s head went with David to Jerusalem,{ac} but the weapons he kept in his own tent.
Saul had been watching David go out against the Philistine, so he asked his army commander Abner, “Abner, whose boy is that?” “As surely as you live, O king, I have no idea,”{ad} Abner said.
“Find out whose boy he is,” the king said.
David returned after killing the Philistine. Abner took him to Saul, and the Philistine’s head was still in David’s hand.
“Whose son are you, young man?” Saul asked. “Your servant Jesse of Bethlehem is my father,” David said.

notes.text: Socoh means “thorny place.” The Greek Old Testament text of chapters 17-18 is much shorter than the Hebrew. The oldest complete Greek copy (Codex Vaticanus) lacks about two-fifths of the Hebrew material, including 17:12-31, 17:41, 17:48b, 17:50, 17:55-18:5, and parts of chapter 18. Scholars debate whether the longer Hebrew text added material or the Greek cut it down.
Ephes-dammim means “edge of blood.”
Elah means “terebinth” or “great tree.”
Hebrew “the man of the between,” meaning a man who fights between two armies in single combat. Same in verse 23.
The meaning of the name Goliath is uncertain.

Hebrew “six cubits and a span,” about 9 feet 9 inches (2.9 meters). The Dead Sea Scroll 4QSam-a (as reported) and the Greek Old Testament read “four cubits and a span,” about 6 feet 9 inches (2 meters). Josephus is also reported to support this. A cubit was about 18 inches (45 centimeters), and a span about 9 inches. This needs scholarly review.
Hebrew “5,000 shekels,” about 125 pounds (57 kilograms).
Or “curved sword.”
Hebrew “600 shekels,” about 15 pounds (6.9 kilograms).
Ephrathite means a man of Ephrathah, the district around Bethlehem (Ruth 1:2; Micah 5:2). The oldest Greek copy lacks verses 12-31 (see the note at verse 1).
So the Greek Old Testament (“looked like an old man among men”) and the Syriac (reported). The Hebrew reads “came among men.”
Hebrew “an ephah,” about 22 liters.
Word for word “ten cuts of milk,” probably cheeses or curds.
Or “and take their pledge,” perhaps a sign that David had delivered the food.
Or “the circle of wagons.”
That is, free from taxes or forced work.
Verses 12-31 are missing from the oldest Greek copy (see the note at verse 1).
So the standard Hebrew text. The Greek Old Testament reads “Let not my lord’s heart sink within him.”
Or “its jaw.” The Greek Old Testament reads “its throat.”
The Greek Old Testament adds, “Shall I not go and strike him and take away a shame from Israel today? For who is this pagan?”
This verse is missing from the Greek Old Testament and from the oldest Greek copy.
The Greek Old Testament adds, “and stones? And David said, No, but worse than a dog.”
So the standard Hebrew text. The Greek Old Testament reads “your limbs and the limbs of the Philistine army.”
The second half of the verse (“David ran fast ... to meet him”) is missing from the Greek Old Testament.
The Greek Old Testament adds “through the helmet.”
This verse is missing from the Greek Old Testament and from the oldest Greek copy.
So the standard Hebrew text. The Greek Old Testament reads “Gath,” which fits the end of the verse.
Shaaraim means “two gates.” The Greek Old Testament reads “the gates.”
Jerusalem was not yet in Israelite hands (see 2 Samuel 5:6-9). The statement may look ahead to a later time.
Verses 55-58 and 18:1-5 are missing from the Greek Old Testament and from the oldest Greek copy (see the note at verse 1).

subheads.55: Saul Asks Whose Son David Is

verses.text: David finished his talk with Saul. From that moment Jonathan’s heart clung to David’s, and Jonathan cared for him as much as for himself.{a}
Saul claimed David that very day. He would not allow David to go home to his father again.
Because Jonathan cared for David as much as for himself, he bound the two of them with a covenant.
Jonathan pulled off the robe he had on and handed it to David. His tunic, sword, bow, and belt went too.
Wherever Saul sent David, David succeeded.{b} So Saul gave him a post over the fighting men, and everyone approved, even Saul’s own officials.

David had killed the Philistine, and the army was on its way home. From every Israelite town, women went out to greet King Saul with song and dance, tambourines, shouts of joy, and three-stringed instruments.{c}
The women answered each other as they played: “Thousands fell to Saul, but ten thousands to David!”
This made Saul furious. The song galled him. “Ten thousands for David,” he said, “and for me just thousands! Nothing remains for him to take but the throne.”{d}
Saul kept a jealous eye on David from that day.{e}
Next day a harmful spirit from God took hold of Saul, and he raved{f} inside the house. David was at his daily job of playing the lyre. Saul had a spear in his hand.
Saul threw it. “I will nail David to the wall,” he thought. Twice David stepped out of its way.
Saul was afraid of David. Yahweh stayed with David but had departed from Saul.{g}
Saul moved David out of his sight by appointing him over a thousand soldiers. David marched them out and marched them home.
Everything David did turned out well, for Yahweh was with him.
Saul noticed David’s great success and dreaded him.
All Israel and Judah, though, loved David, for he was the one who led them out and led them back.

“My older daughter Merab is yours,” Saul told David. “She will be your wife. Only be a brave soldier for me and fight Yahweh’s battles.” Saul thought, “My hand need not touch him. Let the Philistines do the work.”{h}
“Who am I?” David replied to Saul. “What is my family, my father’s clan among the Israelites? Why should I become the king’s son-in-law?”
Saul gave her to Adriel{i} the Meholathite instead.
Another daughter of Saul, Michal, was in love with David. Saul heard this and was glad.
“She will be bait,” he thought. “I will hand her over, and the Philistines will be his downfall.” So Saul spoke to David a second time: “Today you may marry into my family.”{j}
Saul gave his servants their orders: “Talk quietly with David. Tell him, ‘The king likes you, and his whole staff is fond of you. Marry into the royal family.’”
The servants passed this on to David. David answered, “You think it is easy to marry the king’s daughter? I am poor, and nobody of note.”
They carried David’s answer back to Saul.

Saul told them, “Give David this message: ‘The king asks nothing for the bride{k} but a hundred Philistine foreskins. That will avenge him on his enemies.’” Saul hoped David would die at Philistine hands.
When the servants relayed this, David was pleased to become the king’s son-in-law. Before the deadline passed,{l}

he and his men set out and killed two hundred Philistines.{m} David turned in all their foreskins, counted out in full for the king, to win the right to be Saul’s son-in-law. So Saul married his daughter Michal to David.
Saul came to see clearly that Yahweh was with David. He could also see how much Michal, his own daughter, loved David.{n}
This made Saul still more afraid of David. He stayed David’s enemy for good.{o}
Whenever the Philistine commanders marched out to battle, David outdid all of Saul’s officers. His name became well known.{p}

notes.text: Verses 1-5 are missing from the Greek Old Testament and from the oldest Greek copy (see the note at 17:1).
Or “acted wisely.” The Hebrew verb sakal means both. Same in verses 14, 15, and 30.

Hebrew shalishim, perhaps “triangles,” “lutes,” or “three-stringed instruments.” It is uncertain. The Greek Old Testament reads “cymbals.” The Greek lacks “when David returned from striking down the Philistine” and “to meet King Saul,” and reads “to meet David.”
The last sentence is missing from the Greek Old Testament.
Verses 9-11 are missing from the Greek Old Testament and from the oldest Greek copy.
Hebrew “prophesied,” here meaning wild, uncontrolled behavior.
The Greek Old Testament reads only “And Saul was alarmed because of David.”
Verses 17-19 are missing from the Greek Old Testament and from the oldest Greek copy.
Adriel means “my help is God.” Compare 2 Samuel 21:8, where the standard Hebrew text names Michal instead of Merab.
The Hebrew phrase for “a second time” is unclear (word for word “by two”). The last sentence is missing from the Greek Old Testament.
Hebrew mohar, the price a groom paid to the bride’s family.
The last clause (“Before the time was up”) is missing from the Greek Old Testament.
So the standard Hebrew text. The Greek Old Testament reads “a hundred men,” which agrees with verse 25 and with 2 Samuel 3:14.
So the standard Hebrew text. The Greek Old Testament reads “and that all Israel loved him.”
The last clause is missing from the Greek Old Testament.
This verse is missing from the Greek Old Testament and from the oldest Greek copy.

verses.text: Saul ordered his son Jonathan and all his servants to put David to death. Jonathan, though, was deeply attached to David.
Jonathan warned David, “My father Saul wants you dead. Be careful tomorrow morning. Find a place to hide, and do not show yourself.
I will stand next to my father in the field where you hide, and I will bring up your name. Whatever I learn, I will report.”
Jonathan praised David to his father Saul. “Do not harm your servant David, O king,” he said. “He never did you any wrong. His deeds have helped you a great deal.
He risked his life by killing the Philistine, and Yahweh won a great victory for Israel. You saw it and rejoiced. Why bring guilt on yourself by killing an innocent man, David, without cause?”
Saul gave in to Jonathan and took an oath: “I swear by Yahweh’s life that David will not be killed.”
Jonathan summoned David and told him all of this. Then he led David to Saul, and David was in his service as before.
War started again. David marched out against the Philistines and beat them badly. They fled.
One day a harmful spirit from Yahweh came upon Saul as he sat in his house, spear in hand. David was at the lyre.
Saul aimed the spear to nail David against the wall, but David slipped away and the spear drove into the wall. David got clear and fled that night.
Saul posted guards at David’s house to kill him at dawn. But David’s wife Michal told him, “Unless you slip away tonight, you will be dead by morning.”
Michal let David down through a window. He fled and got away.
Michal then took the household idol,{a} laid it on the bed, set a net of goat hair{b} at its head, and spread a cover over it.
Saul’s men arrived to seize David. “He is ill,” she said.
Saul sent them back to look at David. “Bring him to me on the bed,” he said, “and I will kill him.”
The men entered and saw the idol in the bed, the goat-hair net at its head.
Saul said to Michal, “Why did you cheat me like this? You helped my enemy escape!” Michal answered Saul, “He told me, ‘Help me get away, or I will kill you.’”
David fled to Samuel at Ramah and told him all that Saul had done. Then the two of them moved to Naioth.{c}
Saul got word: “David is in Naioth at Ramah.”

Saul sent men to take David. They found a company of prophets in a prophetic trance, with Samuel standing over them as their leader. God’s Spirit came on Saul’s men, and they too fell into a prophetic trance.
Saul learned of this and sent others, and they also went into a trance. He tried a third group, and they did the same.
At last Saul himself set out for Ramah. When he reached the great cistern at Secu,{d} he asked, “Where are Samuel and David?” Someone said, “In Naioth at Ramah.”
He set off for Naioth in Ramah. God’s Spirit came on him as well, and he went on in a trance all the way to Naioth.
He stripped off his clothes too and prophesied in Samuel’s presence. For a whole day and night he lay naked.{e} That is the origin of the saying, “Is Saul one of the prophets?”

notes.text: Hebrew teraphim, small figures of household gods. Here it seems to have been big enough to look like a man. Same in verse 16.
The meaning of the Hebrew is uncertain. The Greek Old Testament reads “the liver of a goat,” from a Hebrew word of similar form.
Naioth may mean “homes” or “pasture camps.” It is uncertain.
So the standard Hebrew text. The Greek Old Testament reads “the well of the threshing floor in Sephi.”
Or “wearing only his underclothes.” The Hebrew word can mean partly clothed.

verses.text: David escaped from Naioth in Ramah and sought out Jonathan. “What have I done?” he said. “What is my crime? What is my offense against your father, that he is after my life?”
“God forbid!” Jonathan said. “You will not die. My father does nothing at all, large or small, without letting me know. Why would he keep this from me? It cannot be.”

But David swore again. “Your father is well aware that you favor me,” he said. “He tells himself, ‘Jonathan must not learn of this, or he will be hurt.’ Yet as Yahweh lives and as you live, only one step separates me from death.”
“Tell me what you want,” Jonathan said. “I will do it.”
“Tomorrow is the new moon,{a}” David said, “and I am supposed to sit at the king’s table. Let me leave and lie low in the open country until the third evening.
If your father asks where I am, say, ‘David pleaded with me for leave to rush to his hometown Bethlehem, since the entire clan is offering its annual sacrifice there.’
If he answers, ‘Good,’ your servant has nothing to fear. If he boils over with rage, know that he has chosen to harm me.
Show kindness to your servant, since you brought me into a covenant with you before Yahweh. Should I be guilty, kill me with your own hand. Why deliver me to your father?”
“Never!” Jonathan said. “If I learned that my father had decided to harm you, would I not tell you?”
“And who will tell me,” David asked, “if your father gives you a harsh reply?”
“Come on,” Jonathan said. “Let us go out into the countryside.” So they both went out.
“By Yahweh, the God of Israel,{b}” said Jonathan, “tomorrow about now, or the day after, I will question my father. If he feels well toward David, I will send you word.
But if my father intends harm to you, may Yahweh strike me hard if I fail to tell you and let you leave in safety. May Yahweh stand by you, as he stood by my father.
And if I am still alive, show me Yahweh’s loyal love{c} so that I do not die.
Never cut off your loyal love from my family, not even when Yahweh removes all David’s enemies from the face of the earth.”
So Jonathan made a pact with David’s family: “May Yahweh call David’s enemies to account.”{d}
Once more Jonathan had David take an oath. He did it out of love, for he loved David as dearly as himself.
Then Jonathan said, “Tomorrow is the new moon, and people will notice your absence. Your chair will sit vacant.
The day after, hurry down{e} to the spot where you hid when this trouble began,{f} and stay by the stone Ezel.{g}
I will shoot three arrows off to the side, as if I were aiming at a target.
Then I will send a boy off to look for them. If I call to him, ‘See, the arrows are this side of you, pick them up,’ you may come out. By Yahweh’s life, you are safe, and nothing is wrong.
But if I say to the boy, ‘The arrows are farther ahead,’ go. Yahweh has sent you away.
And about this agreement between you and me: Yahweh stands between us forever.”
David hid in the field. At the new moon, the king took his place at the feast.
The king sat where he always sat, against the wall. Jonathan faced him,{h} Abner took the seat beside Saul, and David’s place was empty.
Saul said nothing that day. “Something must have happened to him,” he thought. “He must be unclean. Yes, unclean.”{i}
On the second day of the month, David’s place stood empty a second time. Saul asked his son Jonathan, “Why did Jesse’s son miss the meal both yesterday and today?”
Jonathan said to Saul, “David begged me for permission to go off to Bethlehem.

He said, ‘Let me go, I beg you. Our clan is holding a sacrifice in town, and I was ordered by my brother to attend. If you think well of me, let me slip away to visit my brothers.’ That is why he is missing from the king’s table.”

Saul’s anger flared against Jonathan. “You son of a twisted, rebellious mother!{j}” he said. “Do I not know you have taken Jesse’s son as your friend, to your own disgrace and the disgrace of the mother who bore you?
For as long as Jesse’s son lives on the earth, you and your throne will never be safe. Now have him brought to me. He deserves to die!”{k}
“Why must he die?” Jonathan asked his father Saul. “What did he do?”
Saul hurled his spear at Jonathan to hit him. So Jonathan understood: his father had settled on killing David.
Jonathan left the table burning with anger. That second day of the month he would not eat, for he was sick with grief over David, and his father had shamed him.
In the morning Jonathan went to the field for his meeting with David, and a young boy went along.
“Run and find the arrows I am shooting,” he told the boy. The boy ran, and Jonathan shot an arrow over his head.
The boy reached the spot where Jonathan’s arrow had fallen. Jonathan called after him, “The arrow is beyond you, is it not?”
Again Jonathan called, “Go fast! Hurry! Do not stand there!” The boy collected the arrows and returned to his master.
The boy knew nothing. Only Jonathan and David understood what it meant.
Jonathan gave his gear to the boy. “Go on,” he said, “and carry it back to the town.”
After the boy left, David stepped out from beside the south side.{l} He dropped face down on the ground and bowed three times. They kissed and wept with each other, David most of all.{m}

“Go with God’s peace,” Jonathan told David. “We have sworn together in Yahweh’s name: ‘Yahweh stands between me and you, between my children and yours, forever.’” David got up and went off, and Jonathan returned to town.{n}

notes.text: The new moon marked the start of each month. It was a festival day with special meals and sacrifices (Numbers 10:10; 28:11-15).
Hebrew “Yahweh, the God of Israel--.” The oath is unfinished. A verb such as “is witness” may have been lost. This needs scholarly review.
Hebrew hesed, loyal love based on a covenant.
The Hebrew of verses 14-16 is hard. “Enemies of David” may be a scribe’s softening of “David” himself (compare 25:22).
The Hebrew is uncertain, word for word “go down greatly.” The Greek Old Testament reads “you shall stay three days.”
Or “on the day of the business,” probably meaning the events of 19:2-7.
So the standard Hebrew text. Ezel may mean “departure.” The Greek Old Testament reads “beside that mound.”
So the standard Hebrew text. The Greek Old Testament reads “and he went before Jonathan.” Some scholars suggest the original was “Jonathan sat opposite.”
The Greek Old Testament reads “because he has not made himself clean” in place of the repeated clause.
Word for word “son of a perverse woman of rebellion,” an insult aimed at Jonathan himself. The Greek Old Testament reads “son of traitorous young women.”
That is, he must die.
So the Greek Old Testament (“from the mound”), which reflects the mound of verse 19. The Hebrew reads “from beside the south.”
The Hebrew is uncertain.
In Hebrew the last sentence of this verse is 21:1, and 21:1-15 in English is 21:2-16 in Hebrew.

subheads.1: David and Jonathan Make a Plan

verses.text: David arrived at Nob,{a} where Ahimelech{b} the priest lived. Ahimelech came out to meet him, shaking with fear. “Why are you by yourself? Is nobody with you?” he asked.

“The king gave me a job,” David told Ahimelech the priest. “He said, ‘Nobody is to know a thing about the mission I am sending you on or the orders I gave you.’ My men are waiting for me at a certain spot.{c}
So what do you have on hand? Let me have five loaves, or anything else you can find.”
“I have no ordinary bread,” the priest said. “Only holy bread is here. You can have it if your men have stayed away from women.”
“We have kept away from women, as always when I go out on a mission,” David said. “My men’s bodies{d} stay holy even on an ordinary trip. Today they are surely even holier!”{e}
So the priest handed over the holy loaves. No other bread was in the place except the bread of the Presence,{f} which had just been lifted from Yahweh’s table and replaced with warm loaves.
A man in Saul’s service happened to be there that day, held back in front of Yahweh. He was Doeg,{g} an Edomite,{h} and he was in charge of Saul’s shepherds.
David then asked Ahimelech, “Is there a spear or sword you could give me? The king’s business was so pressing that I did not bring along my own sword or any weapon.”

The priest said, “Goliath the Philistine’s sword, the one you killed in the Valley of Elah, is wrapped in cloth behind the ephod. You can have it. It is all there is.” “Nothing compares to it,” David said. “Hand it over.”
David set out that very day, running from Saul, and reached Achish,{i} the king of Gath.
The servants of Achish said, “Is this not David, the king of that country? Did they not dance and sing of him: ‘Saul has slain thousands, but David ten thousands’?”
David kept these words in mind, and fear of Achish, the king of Gath, gripped him.
He changed his conduct as they watched, and played the madman while they held him. He scratched marks{j} on the doors of the gate and drooled into his beard.
“Look at him,” Achish told his officials. “The man is out of his mind. Why bring him to me?
Am I short of madmen? You bring this one to put on a show for me? Should he come into my house?”

notes.text: In Hebrew, 20:42b is numbered 21:1, and 21:1-15 in English is 21:2-16 in Hebrew. Nob was a town of priests near Jerusalem (22:19).
Ahimelech means “my brother is king.” He is probably the same as Ahijah (14:3). Compare Mark 2:26, which names Abiathar.
The Hebrew phrase is deliberately vague (compare Ruth 4:1). The Greek Old Testament reads “in the place called, The faithfulness of God, Phellani Maemoni.”
Or “bodies.” The Hebrew word can mean equipment or the body.
The Hebrew of this verse is hard.
Word for word “bread of the face,” the twelve loaves set before Yahweh in the sanctuary each Sabbath (Leviticus 24:5-9).
Doeg may mean “anxious.” It is uncertain.
So the standard Hebrew text. The Greek Old Testament reads “the Syrian,” a mix-up of the similar Hebrew letters for Edom and Aram. The Greek also reads “tending the mules of Saul.”
The meaning of the name Achish is uncertain. It may be Philistine.
So the standard Hebrew text. The Greek Old Testament reads “drummed upon,” from a Hebrew word of similar form.

verses.text: David slipped away from Gath to the cave of Adullam.{a} When his brothers and all his father’s family learned of it, they came down to him there.
Everyone in trouble, everyone owing money, and everyone with a bitter heart gathered around him. David became their captain, and some four hundred men were with him.
David traveled on to Mizpeh in Moab.{b} He asked the king of Moab, “May my father and mother stay with you, until I learn what God has in store for me?”
He placed them in the care of the king of Moab,{c} and they stayed with him for the entire time David was in the stronghold.
Then the prophet Gad{d} told David, “You must not remain in the stronghold. Move to Judah.” So David left and entered the forest of Hereth.
Someone told Saul that David and his men had been found. Saul was in Gibeah, seated beneath the tamarisk on the hill with his spear in hand, and his servants were standing in a ring around him.
He said to them, “Listen to me, Benjamites! Do you imagine Jesse’s son will give every one of you fields and vineyards, or that he will put you in command of units of a thousand and of a hundred?

Yet all of you conspired against me. When my son made a pact with Jesse’s son, nobody told me. None of you cared enough to warn me that my son had incited my servant to wait in ambush for me, which is just what he is doing.”
Doeg the Edomite, who stood among Saul’s servants, answered, “I watched Jesse’s son arrive at Nob, at the home of Ahimelech son of Ahitub.
Ahimelech consulted Yahweh on his behalf, supplied him with food, and gave him Goliath the Philistine’s sword.”
The king summoned the priest Ahimelech son of Ahitub and every member of his father’s family who served as priests at Nob. They all appeared before the king.
“Now hear me, son of Ahitub,” Saul said. “At your service, my lord,” Ahimelech replied.
“What made you conspire against me, you and this son of Jesse?” Saul said. “You gave him bread and a sword and consulted God for him, so now he rises against me and waits in ambush, as you see.”
The king heard Ahimelech reply, “Which of your servants is as trustworthy as David? He is your own son-in-law, he commands your bodyguard,{e} and your household honors him.
Did I begin consulting God for him only today? Not at all! Let the king not charge your servant or my father’s family with anything. Your servant knew nothing of this, whether little or much.”
“Ahimelech, you will certainly die,” the king said, “you and everyone in your father’s family.”

The king commanded the guards{f} standing by him, “Turn and kill Yahweh’s priests! They have sided with David. They knew he was fleeing and never informed me.” But the king’s servants would not lift a hand to strike Yahweh’s priests.
The king then ordered Doeg, “You, turn and strike the priests.” Doeg the Edomite did so, cutting down eighty-five men{g} who wore the linen ephod on that day.
He also put Nob, the priests’ town, to the sword: men and women, children and nursing babies, as well as oxen, donkeys, and sheep.
A son of Ahimelech son of Ahitub, Abiathar{h} by name, was the only one to get away. He ran off after David.
Abiathar informed David that Saul had killed Yahweh’s priests.
David said to Abiathar, “When I spotted Doeg the Edomite there that day, I knew he would surely tell Saul. I caused the deaths{i} of your whole father’s family.
Remain with me and fear nothing. Whoever hunts your life hunts mine, and with me you will be protected.”

notes.text: Adullam was a town in the lowland of Judah, about 16 miles southwest of Jerusalem. Its name may mean “refuge.” It is uncertain.
Mizpeh means “watchtower.”

So the Syriac and the Latin Vulgate. The Hebrew reads “he led them” (read with other vowels). The Greek Old Testament reads “he persuaded the king of Moab.” David’s great-grandmother Ruth was from Moab (Ruth 4:17).
Gad means “good fortune.”
The Hebrew is uncertain, word for word “and turns aside to your obedience.” It is often taken to mean “captain over your bodyguard.” The Greek Old Testament reads “carrying out all your orders.”
Hebrew ratsim, the king’s guards who ran in front of his chariot.
So the standard Hebrew text. The Greek Old Testament reads “three hundred and five men.”
Abiathar means “the father is abundant” or “father of plenty.” It is uncertain.
So the Greek Old Testament (“I am guilty of the death”) and the Latin Vulgate. The Hebrew reads “I have turned against,” from a verb of similar form.

subheads.1: David in the Cave of Adullam

verses.text: David was told, “The Philistines are fighting against Keilah{a} and plundering the threshing floors.”
David consulted Yahweh: “Shall I go and strike these Philistines?” Yahweh told him, “Go. Strike the Philistines and rescue Keilah.”
David’s men objected, “Here in Judah we are already scared. It will be far worse if we march to Keilah against the Philistine forces!”
David consulted Yahweh once more. Yahweh replied, “Go down to Keilah at once. I am delivering the Philistines into your hands.”
So David marched with his men to Keilah and fought the Philistines. He drove off their herds and dealt them a heavy blow. That is how David rescued the people of Keilah.
Now Abiathar son of Ahimelech had run to David at Keilah, bringing an ephod down with him.{b}
When Saul was told that David had gone into Keilah, he said, “God has delivered him to me.{c} He has boxed himself in, entering a town with gates and bars.”
Saul summoned his entire army to war, to march down against Keilah and close in on David and his men.
David found out about Saul’s evil scheme. He said to Abiathar the priest, “Fetch the ephod.”
David prayed, “Yahweh, God of Israel, your servant has been told that Saul means to march on Keilah and wreck it for my sake.
Will Keilah’s citizens{d} give me up to him? Will Saul come down, as your servant was told? Yahweh, God of Israel, answer your servant, I beg you.” Yahweh said, “He will come down.”
David asked, “And will the citizens of Keilah give me and my men up to Saul?” “They will give you up,” Yahweh said.
David and his men, about six hundred in all, then left Keilah and drifted wherever they could. Word reached Saul that David had slipped out of Keilah, so he dropped the plan to march.
David camped in the wilderness at hard-to-reach spots, and stayed in the hill country of the wilderness of Ziph.{e} Day after day Saul hunted him, but God did not let Saul have him.
David saw{f} that Saul had marched out to take his life. At the time David was in Horesh,{g} in the wilderness of Ziph.
Saul’s son Jonathan set off to find David at Horesh. There he helped David trust God and take heart.
“Fear nothing,” he told David. “My father Saul’s hand will never find you. Israel will be yours to rule, and I will stand second to you. My father Saul understands this as well.”
The two made a covenant in Yahweh’s presence. Then Jonathan went back home, while David remained in Horesh.
Some Ziphites traveled to Saul at Gibeah. “Is David not hiding among us?” they asked. “He is in the strongholds of Horesh, on Hachilah hill south of Jeshimon.{h}
Whenever you like, O king, come down. Delivering him into the king’s hands will be our job.”
“Yahweh bless you,” Saul said, “for showing me such sympathy.
Go and make further preparations. Find out precisely where his feet take him and who has seen him there, since I hear he is extremely cunning.
Study each of the hideouts where he lurks, then come back with sure facts.{i} After that I will go along, and should he be in the country, I will hunt him down in every Judean clan.”
They left and reached Ziph before Saul did. David and his men meanwhile were in the wilderness of Maon,{j} in the Arabah south of Jeshimon.
Saul went with his men to search. David was warned and went down to the rock,{k} where he stayed in the wilderness of Maon. Hearing this, Saul followed David into that wilderness.
Saul walked along one flank of the mountain while David and his men walked along the other. David was rushing to escape, for Saul and his men were circling to capture David’s group.
A messenger reached Saul. “Hurry back!” he said. “The Philistines have raided the country.”
Saul broke off the pursuit of David and marched against the Philistines. For this reason the place got the name Rock of Divisions.{l}
David went up from there and made his home in the strongholds of En-gedi.{m}

notes.text: Keilah was a town in the lowland of Judah, about 3 miles south of Adullam.
The Greek Old Testament reads “he went down with David to Keilah, having an ephod in his hand.”
Or “made him a stranger to himself.” The Hebrew verb usually means “estrange.” The Greek Old Testament reads “sold him.”
Or “lords” (Hebrew baale). Same in verse 12.
Ziph was a town in the hill country of Judah, about 4 miles southeast of Hebron.
Or “was afraid.” The Hebrew letters can be read either way.
Or “in the woods.” Horesh means “wood” or “thicket.”
Jeshimon means “wasteland,” the barren land west of the Dead Sea.
Or “at a set time.” The Hebrew is uncertain.
Maon was a town about 8 miles south of Hebron.
Or “to Sela.”
Hebrew Sela-hammahlekoth, maybe “Rock of Escape” or “Rock of Divisions.” It is uncertain. The Greek Old Testament reads “the divided Rock.”
En-gedi means “spring of the young goat,” an oasis on the west shore of the Dead Sea. In Hebrew this verse is 24:1, and 24:1-22 in English is 24:2-23 in Hebrew.

verses.text: Saul came back from chasing the Philistines. Someone told him, “David is in the wilderness of En-gedi.”{a}
Saul picked three thousand of Israel’s finest soldiers and marched off to look for David and his men, in the area of the Rocks of the Wild Goats.{b}
By the road were some sheep pens with a cave beside them. Saul went inside to relieve himself.{c} David and his men were sitting far back in that same cave.

David’s men murmured, “Here is the day Yahweh spoke of when he said, ‘Your enemy is mine to give you; treat him however you see fit.’” David tiptoed forward and snipped off a corner of Saul’s robe without a sound.
Afterward David felt guilty for cutting off the corner of Saul’s robe.{d}
“May Yahweh never let me do this to my master,” he said to his men. “He is Yahweh’s anointed. I will not raise my hand against him.”
Using such words, David restrained his men and kept them from jumping Saul. Saul stood up and walked out of the cave and on along the road.
Then David left the cave and shouted to Saul, “My lord the king!” Saul looked behind him. David bent down to the ground, face first, and paid him respect.
“Why listen to those who tell you, ‘David wants to hurt you’?” David said to Saul.

“You have just seen for yourself that Yahweh placed you in my hands inside the cave. Some men urged me to kill you, but I{e} showed you mercy. ‘I will not lay a hand on my master,’ I said, ‘because he is Yahweh’s anointed.’

Look, my father! See the corner of your robe I am holding. I cut it off but did not kill you. Let that show you I mean no harm and no rebellion. I never wronged you, yet you are hunting me to end my life.
Let Yahweh judge between us. Let Yahweh punish you for what you do to me. My own hand will never touch you.
An old saying goes, ‘Wicked deeds come from wicked people.’ My hand will never touch you.
Whom is the king of Israel chasing? Whom are you after? A dead dog! A lone flea!
Let Yahweh be the judge and decide between us. May he look at my case, argue it, and free me from your power.”{f}
David finished speaking to Saul, and Saul said, “Is that your voice, David my son?” Then Saul broke down and wept aloud.
“You are more honest than I am,” he told David. “You paid me back with kindness, though I paid you back with cruelty.
Today you showed how good you were to me. Yahweh put me in your power, and you did not kill me.
When someone finds his enemy, does he send him off unharmed? May Yahweh reward you with good for what you did for me today.
I know now that you will certainly be king, and that Israel’s kingdom will stand firm in your hands.
So swear to me by Yahweh that you will not kill off my children after me or wipe my name out of my father’s family.”
David gave Saul his oath. Saul went home, and David and his men climbed to the stronghold.{g}

notes.text: In Hebrew, 24:1-22 is numbered 24:2-23 (see the note at 23:29).
Hebrew “the Rocks of the Ibexes” (wild mountain goats). The Greek Old Testament reads “in front of Saddaeem,” taking it as a place name.
Word for word “to cover his feet,” a polite expression.
The Hebrew reads “Saul’s corner,” meaning the corner of his robe. Cutting the corner of a robe may have stood for taking away his royal authority (compare 15:27-28).
So the Greek Old Testament (“I would not kill you, but spared you”) and other ancient copies. The Hebrew reads “but it spared you,” perhaps meaning “my eye spared you.”
Or “rescue me from your hand.”
The Greek Old Testament reads “the stronghold of Messera,” taking the Hebrew word for “stronghold” as a place name.

verses.text: Samuel died, and all Israel met to grieve for him. His body was laid to rest in his own house in Ramah. David moved on to the wilderness of Paran.{a}
In Maon lived a man whose business was at Carmel.{b} He owned three thousand sheep and a thousand goats, which made him very wealthy, and he was in Carmel to shear them.
The man was Nabal,{c} and Abigail{d} was his wife. She had good sense and a lovely face. He was a rough, ill-tempered man from the family of Caleb.{e}
In the wilderness David heard that Nabal was shearing sheep.
He sent ten of his young men with this order: “Go up to Carmel, find Nabal, and greet him for me.
Tell him: ‘Long life!{f} Peace to you, to your household, and to all you own.
I hear that you are shearing. Your shepherds stayed near us, and we never harmed them. Nothing of theirs was lost the whole time they were at Carmel.
Ask your own young men; they will tell you. So be kind to my young men, because we have come at a time of celebration.{g} Whatever you can spare, give to your servants and to your son David.’”
David’s young men gave Nabal this whole message in David’s name. Then they waited.
Nabal replied, “Who is David? Who is this Jesse’s son? Lately many a servant has been breaking away from his master.
Am I supposed to hand my bread and water, and the meat I slaughtered for my shearers, to strangers from who knows where?”
David’s young men turned around, went back, and told him all of it.
“Put on your swords, all of you!” David said. Each man buckled on his sword, David too. Some four hundred men marched with David, while two hundred remained to guard the gear.
A servant took the news to Abigail, Nabal’s wife. “David sent men from the wilderness with greetings for our master, and he hurled abuse at them.
Those men were very good to us. They never harmed us, and nothing of ours went missing the whole time we were with them in the fields.
Night and day they were a wall around us while we tended the sheep near them.
So think it over and decide what to do. Ruin is planned for our master and all his household. Nobody can reason with him, he is such a scoundrel.”{h}
Abigail moved fast. She took two hundred loaves, two wineskins, five dressed sheep, a bushel of roasted grain,{i} a hundred bunches of raisins, and two hundred fig cakes. All this she put on donkeys.
“Go ahead of me,” she told her servants. “I will follow you.” She said nothing to her husband Nabal.
Riding her donkey, she came down by a track screened by the mountain. There were David and his men, coming down the other way, and she ran into them.
David had just been saying, “I guarded this man’s property in the wilderness for nothing. Not one thing of his was lost, and he has repaid me with evil in place of good.
May God deal with David{j} again and again if one single male{k} belonging to Nabal is still alive at sunrise.”
When Abigail caught sight of David, she slid down from the donkey and threw herself down in front of him, her face to the ground.
At his feet she said, “Let the blame fall on me, my lord, on me. Please let your servant speak, and listen to what she says.
My lord, pay no attention to Nabal, that scoundrel. He is exactly what his name says. His name means fool, and he lives up to it. I, your servant, did not see the men you sent, my lord.
My lord, by the life of Yahweh and by your life, Yahweh has stopped you from shedding blood and from settling the score yourself. Let your enemies and anyone who tries to hurt you become like Nabal.
Let this gift{l} your servant has brought to you, my lord, be given to the young men who follow you.
Please forgive your servant’s offense. Yahweh will surely build my lord a lasting dynasty, because my lord fights Yahweh’s battles. No wrong will be found in you as long as you live.

Even if somebody pursues you and aims at your life, my lord’s life is safely tied up in the bundle of the living{m} beside Yahweh your God. Your enemies’ lives he will sling away, as a stone leaves the pocket of a sling.
When Yahweh has done for you, my lord, all the good he promised and has made you leader over Israel,
you will not be troubled or have a guilty heart for shedding blood for no reason or for taking revenge yourself. When Yahweh has treated my lord well, remember your servant.”
“Blessed be Yahweh, the God of Israel, who sent you to meet me today!” David said to Abigail.
“Bless you for your good sense. Bless you for stopping me today from murder and from avenging myself with my own hand.
I swear by the living Yahweh, the God of Israel, who held me back from hurting you: had you not hurried to meet me, Nabal would have had no male left by dawn.”
David took the gift from her. “Go back to your house in peace,” he said. “I heard what you said and I will do as you ask.”{n}
Abigail went back to Nabal. He was throwing a banquet at home, as grand as a king’s. Nabal was cheerful and very drunk, so she told him nothing until dawn.
Next morning, with the wine gone out of him, Nabal heard it all from his wife. His heart sank and he went stiff as a rock.
Roughly ten days passed. Then Yahweh hit Nabal, and Nabal was dead.

David heard that Nabal was dead. “Blessed be Yahweh,” he said. “He has answered the insult from Nabal and kept me from doing wrong. Yahweh made Nabal pay for his evil.” Then David sent word to Abigail, asking her to marry him.
David’s servants came to Abigail at Carmel. “David has sent us to fetch you for him, to be his wife,” they said.
She rose, bent low to the ground, and said, “Here is your servant, ready to wash the feet of my lord’s servants.”
Abigail got ready in haste, mounted a donkey, and left with five of her maids walking behind. She followed David’s messengers and became his wife.
David had also taken Ahinoam from Jezreel{o} as a wife, so now he had two.
Saul had given Michal, his daughter and David’s wife, to a man named Palti{p} son of Laish, from Gallim.

notes.text: So the standard Hebrew text. The Greek Old Testament reads “Maon,” as in verse 2.
This Carmel (meaning “garden land” or “orchard”) was a town in Judah near Maon, about 7 miles south of Hebron. It is not Mount Carmel in the north.
Nabal means “fool” (see verse 25). The word suggests a person who is morally senseless.
Abigail may mean “my father is joy.” It is uncertain.

Or “according to his heart.” The Hebrew letters can be read either way. Calebites were descendants of Caleb, who received the region of Hebron (Joshua 14:13-14). The Greek Old Testament reads “a man of a dog-like nature,” a play on the name Caleb, which sounds like the word for “dog.”
The Hebrew is uncertain, word for word “to the living one.”
A feast day, the time of sheep-shearing.
Hebrew “a son of Belial.” Same in verse 25.
Hebrew “five seahs,” about 33 quarts; a seah was about a third of an ephah. The Greek Old Testament reads “five ephahs of fine flour” and “one homer of dried grapes” in place of the hundred clusters.
So the Greek Old Testament (“So God do to David”). The Hebrew reads “to the enemies of David,” apparently a scribe’s change to keep a curse from falling on David himself.
Hebrew “one who urinates against a wall,” a coarse way to say a male. Same in verse 34.
Hebrew “blessing.”
A picture of a life kept safe like a treasure tied in a bundle.
That is, “granted your request.”
Ahinoam means “my brother is pleasantness.” This Jezreel was a town in Judah (Joshua 15:56), not the northern city.
Called Paltiel in 2 Samuel 3:15. Palti means “my deliverance”; Paltiel means “God is my deliverance.” Gallim was a town near Gibeah (Isaiah 10:30).

verses.text: Some Ziphites came to Saul at Gibeah with a report: “David is hiding on Hachilah hill, which looks toward Jeshimon.”
Saul set out for the wilderness of Ziph, taking along three thousand of Israel’s best men to look for David there.
Saul made camp by the road on Hachilah hill, across from Jeshimon. David was living out in the wilderness, and he noticed that Saul had followed him there.
He sent out spies, who confirmed that Saul really had come.{a}

David walked to the place where Saul’s camp stood. He could see where Saul slept, and Abner son of Ner,{b} the army commander. Saul slept in the middle of the camp,{c} and the soldiers were bedded down around him.
David put a question to Ahimelech the Hittite and to Abishai{d} the son of Zeruiah, who was Joab’s brother: “Which of you will come with me into Saul’s camp?” “I will,” said Abishai.

David and Abishai entered the camp at night. There lay Saul, fast asleep in the middle of it, his spear driven into the earth beside his head. Abner and the soldiers lay sleeping in a circle around him.
Abishai whispered to David, “Your enemy is God’s gift to you today. With this spear I can fix him to the ground with a single blow. A second one will not be needed.”
“Do not harm him,” David said. “Who could strike Yahweh’s anointed and go unpunished?
By the life of Yahweh,” David went on, “Yahweh himself will deal with him. Perhaps his day will come and he will die, or perhaps he will go into battle and be killed.
Yahweh forbid that I lift a hand against his anointed. Pick up the spear beside his head and the water jug, and we will go.”
So David picked up the spear and water jug beside Saul’s head, and the two slipped away. Nobody saw it, nobody knew, and nobody stirred. Yahweh had made them all sink into a heavy sleep.
David crossed to the far side and took his stand on a hilltop some distance off, with a wide gap between them.
He shouted toward the soldiers and Abner son of Ner: “Do you hear me, Abner?” “Who is it that is calling out to the king?” Abner answered.
David said to Abner, “You are a man, are you not? Who in Israel can match you? So why did you fail to protect the king, your lord? A soldier entered the camp to destroy him.

What you have done is wrong. By the life of Yahweh, you all deserve death,{e} since you failed to protect your master, Yahweh’s anointed. Now look around. The king’s spear is missing, and so is the water jug that stood by his head!”
Saul knew the voice. “Is that you, David my son?” “Yes, my lord the king, it is,” David said.
“Why does my lord keep chasing his servant? What have I done? What wrong have I committed?

My lord the king, please hear your servant out. If Yahweh set you against me, let an offering soothe him.{f} But if men did it, may Yahweh curse them! They have chased me away today from my share of Yahweh’s land, telling me, ‘Go and worship other gods.’
Let my blood not spill on the ground, far from where Yahweh is. The king of Israel has set out to hunt a single flea,{g} the way someone hunts a partridge on the hills.”
“I have sinned,” Saul said. “Come home, David my son. Never again will I harm you, because my life mattered to you today. I have acted like a fool and gone badly wrong.”
“Here is the king’s spear,” David replied.{h} “Have one of your young men cross over and fetch it.
Yahweh rewards every man for his goodness and loyalty. Today Yahweh gave you to me, yet I refused to harm Yahweh’s anointed.
Just as I held your life dear today, may Yahweh hold mine dear and save me from all trouble.”
“May you be blessed, David my son,” said Saul. “You will accomplish great things and come out the winner.” David went on his way, and Saul returned home.

notes.text: Or “had come to Nacon.” It is uncertain. The Hebrew word can be read as a place name.
Abner may mean “my father is a lamp.” It is uncertain. Ner means “lamp.”
Or “inside the circle of wagons.” Same in verse 7.
Ahimelech means “my brother is king.” Abishai may mean “my father is a gift.” It is uncertain. Zeruiah, David’s sister (1 Chronicles 2:16), was the mother of Abishai, Joab, and Asahel.
Hebrew “you are sons of death.”
Word for word “let him smell an offering,” that is, let a sacrifice calm him.
The Greek Old Testament reads “to seek your life” instead of “one flea” (compare 24:14).
So the traditional Hebrew reading (qere). The written text (ketiv) reads “Here is the king’s spear.”

verses.text: Inwardly David reasoned, “Someday Saul is going to finish me. Nothing is wiser than slipping off to the Philistines’ country. Saul will tire of combing Israel’s borders for me, and I will have escaped his grasp.”
So David crossed over with the six hundred men who followed him, and came to Maoch’s son Achish, who ruled Gath.
At Gath, David stayed under Achish’s protection. His men came too, each one bringing his household. David brought both his wives, Ahinoam from Jezreel, and Nabal’s widow Abigail, from Carmel.
Saul heard that David had escaped to Gath, and he gave up the chase.

Then David spoke to Achish: “If I have earned your good opinion, let me have a spot in some town out in the countryside, where I can settle. A servant like me has no business sharing the royal city with you.”
On that very day Achish handed Ziklag{a} to him. So to this day Ziklag is held by Judah’s kings.
In all, David spent one year and four months{b} on Philistine soil.

During that time David and his men went on raids against the Geshurites, the Girzites,{c} and the Amalekites. Those tribes had been living in the land since ancient days, from Shur stretching to Egypt.
Whenever David struck a region, nobody survived there, man or woman. He carried off flocks, herds, donkeys, camels, and garments, and came back to Achish.
Achish would ask, “Whom did you raid this time?” David’s replies were: “The Negeb of Judah,” or “The Negeb of the Jerahmeelites,” or “The Negeb of the Kenites.”{d}

David spared no man or woman, so none could be taken to Gath. His reasoning was, “They could tell on us, saying, ‘David did this.’” That was how he behaved all the months he lived in the Philistine country.
Achish believed in David. He told himself, “His own people Israel must hate him by now. He will serve me for the rest of his days.”

notes.text: Ziklag was a town in the Negeb, in southern Judah. Its exact location is uncertain.
Hebrew “days and four months”; “days” here means a year. The Greek Old Testament reads “four months.”
So the standard written Hebrew text (ketiv). The margin reads “Gezrites.” Some Greek manuscripts lack this name.
Hebrew “the Negeb,” meaning “dry land,” the southern region of Judah.

verses.text: Around that time the Philistines gathered their armies to fight Israel. “You must know that you and your men will march out with me in the army,” Achish told David.
David replied, “Then you will find out what your servant can do.” Achish said, “Good. I appoint you as my permanent guard.{a}”

By now Samuel had died. All of Israel had grieved for him and laid him to rest at Ramah, the town where he lived. Saul had also banished from the land every person who called up the dead or consulted spirits.{b}
The Philistines came together and camped at Shunem.{c} Saul gathered all Israel and camped at Gilboa.{d}
Saul looked at the Philistine army and was terrified. His heart pounded.
Saul asked Yahweh what to do, but Yahweh gave no answer, whether by dreams, by the Urim, or by prophets.
“Find me a woman who talks to spirits,{e}” Saul told his servants. “I will go and ask her.” “There is one at En-dor,{f}” they said.
Disguising himself in other garments, Saul set out at night with two men and came to the woman. “Please call up a spirit for me,” he said, “and bring up whoever I tell you.”
The woman said, “Surely you have heard what Saul did. He cut off the mediums and spirit-seekers from the land. Are you trying to catch me in a snare so I will be put to death?”
Saul gave her his oath in Yahweh’s name: “By the living Yahweh, no harm will come to you over this.”
“Whom should I bring up?” the woman asked. “Samuel,” he said. “Bring him up for me.”
The woman saw Samuel and screamed. “Why did you trick me?” she said to Saul. “You are Saul!”
“Do not be afraid,” the king said. “What do you see?” “A god-like being{g} is coming up from the ground,” she told Saul.
“What is his shape?” he asked. She said, “It is an old man rising, and he wears a robe.” Saul understood that this was Samuel. He knelt, face on the ground, and bowed.

Samuel said to Saul, “Why did you disturb my rest by summoning me?” “I am in desperate trouble,” Saul replied. “Philistines are attacking me, and God has turned away. Neither prophets nor dreams bring me an answer now. That is why I summoned you, so you could tell me what to do.”
“Why ask me,” Samuel said, “when Yahweh has left you and become your enemy?{h}
Yahweh is doing to you{i} exactly what he announced through me. He has taken the kingdom from your grasp and handed it to someone close to you, David.
You did not listen to Yahweh. You never carried out his burning anger on the Amalekites. For that reason Yahweh brings this on you today.
Yahweh will also give both Israel and you into Philistine power. By this time tomorrow you and your sons will be at my side. Israel’s army, too, Yahweh will turn over to the Philistines.”
At once Saul collapsed, stretched flat on the ground, filled with dread at what Samuel had said. His strength was gone, since he had taken no food that day or that night.
The woman walked up to Saul and saw him badly frightened. “Sir, your maidservant obeyed you,” she said. “I put my own life at risk and did what you asked of me.
Now you listen to me, too. Allow me to put some food before you. Eat, so you can get your strength back before you go on your way.”
He said no: “I won’t eat.” But his men, along with the woman, kept pressing him. At last he listened. He rose off the ground and sat on the bed.
In her house the woman kept a well-fed calf. She hurried to butcher it. She also took flour, worked it into dough, and baked it without yeast.
She brought it all to Saul and his men, and they ate. Before dawn they rose and went off into the night.

notes.text: That is, “my bodyguard.”
Hebrew ovot and yidde’onim, those who claimed to consult the spirits of the dead. Same in verse 9.
Shunem was a town in the land of Issachar, on the slope of the hill of Moreh.
Gilboa was a mountain ridge south of the Jezreel Valley.
Hebrew “a woman who is mistress of a spirit” (ba’alat ov).
En-dor means “spring of the dwelling” (uncertain), a town north of the hill of Moreh.
Or “a godlike being” or “divine beings” (Hebrew elohim, with a plural verb). The Greek Old Testament reads “gods coming up out of the earth.”
The Hebrew word ar is uncertain. It may mean “adversary” (an Aramaic sense). The Greek Old Testament reads “is with your neighbor.”
So many Hebrew manuscripts and the Greek Old Testament. The standard text reads “to him,” meaning David.

subheads.3: Saul and the Medium at En-dor

verses.text: The Philistines massed all their troops at Aphek.{a} The Israelites had pitched their tents beside the spring at Jezreel.
The Philistine chiefs were filing past in companies of a hundred and a thousand. At the very back, next to Achish, walked David and his men.

The Philistine officers asked, “Why are these Hebrews here?” Achish told them, “That is David, an official of Saul, Israel’s king. He has stayed with me over a year now, and since he deserted to me I have seen no flaw in him.”

The Philistine officers grew furious with Achish. “Make that man go back to the town you assigned him,” they said. “He is not marching into battle with us. He might change sides{b} during the fight. What would win his master back faster than our soldiers’ heads?
Is he not the David they sang of while they danced: ‘Saul has killed his thousands, and David has killed his ten thousands’?”

Achish summoned David. “By the living Yahweh,{c} you have been upright,” he said. “I would gladly have you march with my army. In all your time with me I have seen no fault in you. Yet the other lords will not accept you.
Turn around and go home quietly. Do nothing that offends the Philistine lords.”
David protested, “What wrong did I do? What have you seen in your servant since I entered your service that stops me from fighting my lord the king’s enemies?”
Achish answered, “I admit that in my eyes you are as pure as an angel{d} of God. Still, the Philistine officers insist: ‘He must not go up to the battle with us.’
So get up at dawn, you and your master’s servants who came with you,{e} and leave when it gets light.”
At dawn David and his men set out on the road back to Philistine country. The Philistines marched up to Jezreel.

notes.text: Aphek was a town in the Sharon plain, the gathering place before the battle of 4:1.
Hebrew satan, “adversary.”
A Philistine king swearing by Yahweh may be a courtesy toward David.
Or “messenger.”
The Greek Old Testament adds “and go to the place where I put you, and do not think evil in your heart, for you are good in my sight.”

verses.text: David and his men got to Ziklag after three days. Amalekites had struck the Negeb. They had hit Ziklag and set it on fire.
Every woman there, and everybody else, high and low, had been captured. No one had been killed. The raiders simply drove them off.
David and his men came to the town and found it burned. Their wives, sons, and daughters were gone, taken as captives.
David and the men with him cried out loud and wept until they had no strength left to weep.
David’s two wives had been taken too: Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail, the widow of Nabal of Carmel.
David was in deep trouble, because the men talked of stoning him. They were all bitter over their sons and daughters. But David found strength in Yahweh his God.
“Bring me the ephod, please,” David told Abiathar the priest, son of Ahimelech. Abiathar brought it to him.
David asked Yahweh, “Should I go after this raiding band? Will I overtake them?” “Go after them,” Yahweh answered. “You will overtake them and rescue the captives.”
David set out with his six hundred men. They reached the Besor ravine,{a} and there the stragglers halted.
David kept on with four hundred men. Two hundred stayed, too worn out to cross the Besor ravine.
Out in a field they came upon an Egyptian man and took him to David. They fed him some bread and let him drink water.
They also offered him a lump of pressed figs and two clusters of raisins. He ate and revived. For three days and three nights he had had nothing to eat or drink.
“Who is your master, and what place are you from?” David asked. “I am a young Egyptian, servant to an Amalekite,” he answered. “My owner dropped me three days back, since I took ill.
Our raid hit the southern Cherethites,{b} some of Judah’s territory, and the southern part of Caleb’s land. Ziklag we set on fire.”
David asked, “Will you take me down to that gang?” He answered, “Promise me before God that you won’t put me to death or hand me back to my owner, and I will take you to them.”
He guided David down, and there lay the Amalekites, sprawled across the countryside, feasting and drinking and dancing for joy over the enormous haul from the Philistine and Judean territories.
David struck them from dusk to the evening of the following day.{c} Only four hundred young men escaped, mounted on camels.
Everything the Amalekites had seized, David recovered, and his two wives as well.
None of it was lost, whether small or large, sons or daughters, spoil or other captured items. David returned with all of it.
David gathered the flocks and herds too. The men led them ahead of the rest of the animals, calling out, “This is David’s spoil!”{d}

When David reached the two hundred, those who had been too exhausted to go along and were left at the Besor ravine, they came forward to welcome him and the men with him. David walked up and asked how they were.
Every nasty, worthless man{e} among David’s companions objected: “Those two hundred did not march with us. They get none of the goods we recovered. Let them each take wife and children and go.”
“No, my brothers,” David said. “Do not do this with what Yahweh has given us. He kept us safe and handed over the raiders who attacked us.
Nobody will agree with you here. The one who waits with the supplies gets what the one who fights gets. Everyone divides equally.”
From that day on David made this a rule and law for Israel, and it is still so.
When David reached Ziklag, he sent some of the loot to his friends, the elders of Judah. “Here is a gift{f} for you from the plunder of Yahweh’s enemies,” he said.
He sent it to those in Bethel, Ramoth in the Negeb, and Jattir;
to the people in Aroer, Siphmoth, and Eshtemoa,
to the people in Racal and the Jerahmeelite towns, and to the Kenite towns,
to those in Hormah, Bor-ashan,{g} and Athach;
and to those in Hebron, and everywhere David and his men had gone.

notes.text: Besor was a stream (a wadi) south of Ziklag, flowing west to the Mediterranean Sea.
The Cherethites were a people related to the Philistines, perhaps from Crete. Some of them later served in David’s bodyguard (2 Samuel 8:18).
The Hebrew is uncertain, word for word “from the twilight until the evening of their next day.”
The Hebrew of this verse is hard.
Hebrew “men of Belial.”
Hebrew “blessing.”
So many Hebrew manuscripts. Others read “Cor-ashan.” Bor-ashan means “smoking pit.”

verses.text: Meanwhile the Philistines battled Israel. The Israelites turned and ran, and a great number were struck down on Mount Gilboa.
Pressing close to Saul and his sons, the Philistines killed three of the sons: Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchi-shua.{a}
The fighting grew fierce around Saul. Archers found him and wounded him badly.{b}

“Draw your sword and run me through,” Saul ordered his armor-bearer, “before these uncircumcised brutes get to me and abuse me.” The armor-bearer refused, in terror. Then Saul grabbed the sword himself and threw himself on its point.
When the young man understood that Saul had died, he too threw himself on his sword and died beside him.
So Saul, his three sons, his armor-bearer, and all his men died together that same day.

People of Israel on the far side of the valley and beyond the Jordan learned that the troops had fled and that Saul and his sons had died. They deserted their towns and escaped, and Philistines moved in to live there.
The day after, Philistines arrived to rob the dead. On Mount Gilboa they found Saul and his three sons, fallen.
They cut off his head and took his armor. They sent messengers all over the Philistine land to spread the news in the temples of their idols and among their people.
They placed his weapons in the temple of the Ashtoreths{c} and fastened his corpse to Beth-shan’s wall.{d}
The people of Jabesh-gilead heard what the Philistines had done to Saul.
Every brave man rose and marched through the night. They lifted down the bodies of Saul and his sons from Beth-shan’s wall, carried them back to Jabesh, and burned them there.{e}
Their bones they buried under the tamarisk at Jabesh, and they went without food for seven days.

notes.text: Abinadab means “my father is generous.” Malchi-shua means “my king is salvation.” It is uncertain.
Or “he was very afraid of the archers.” The Greek Old Testament reads “he was wounded under the ribs.”
The plural of Ashtoreth (Astarte), a Canaanite goddess. The Greek Old Testament reads “the temple of Astarte.” First Chronicles 10:10 adds that they fastened his head in the temple of Dagon.
Beth-shan means “house of quiet” (uncertain), a city where the Jezreel and Jordan valleys meet.
Burning bodies was not the usual Israelite practice. Some think the verb here may mean “anointed with spices” (scholars still discuss this). First Chronicles 10:12 does not mention the burning.
